PRIVILEGE-MR. COLDWELL REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 24
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in accordance with the rules of the house and as my right I wish to direct your attention to a speech made by the Minister of National War Services (Mr. LaFleche) on Friday evening. I asked you to get a transcript to see what the record had to say. At page 901 of Hansard the Minister is reported as having said:
' Well, to take the trouble to protect oneself by slipping in the word "alleged" when one has nothing plain in one's heart is not the act of a brave man, and I regret very much to say this, but actions of that kind remind me that it is well in war time to act the man even though one has not chosen to go to meet the enemy. I have no admiration for men who do nothing of which I know to help to win the war, but remain at home, perhaps not willingly yet effectively, to cause trouble in a family which should remain united so that we can do a better job in helping the other united nations in downing our enemies.
I then said:
I rise to a point of order. Is the hon. gentlemen not casting an innuendo with an imputation reflecting upon the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre?
Privilege-Mr. Coldwell

And the minister said:
And the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar.
I particularly wish to draw your attention to the accusation hurled across the floor of this house that we of this party are national socialists. On page 902 of Hansard the minister is reported as having said this:
The same hon. gentleman expressed some fear that this country might some day be governed under nationalist socialism. Well, I wish to give him my assurance in that respect again.
And I interjected: "Nor do I." Then the minister said:
We now have the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar expressing publicly in this house the view, the opinion, that he will never come to power.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. COLDWELL REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 24
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. COLDWELL REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 24
speechtext:
May I just interject to say that in my opinion this applause for that kind of statement is unseemly in this house. Then at page 902 the minister is reported as having said:
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar does not like to be called, or his party to be called, national socialists, despite what has been said many times and despite that his lieutenant in British Columbia preached the methods employed by that party in Germany of which our friend says he is not a-
The record breaks there. Mr. Speaker, I contend that we are at war with national socialism in Germany, and to endeavour to attack any party in this country as being a national socialist movement is to accuse that party of disloyalty to this country and falsely to imply a position which is not borne out by the facts. May I say that this movement in its philosophy and outlook is exactly the same as the labour and socialist parties of Great Britain, Australia, New Zealand and other countries.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. COLDWELL REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 24
speechtext: That is your opinion.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. COLDWELL REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 24
speechtext: That is just not true.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. COLDWELL REFERENCE TO REMARKS IN DEBATE ON FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 24

I should like to get your ruling, Mr. Speaker.
Hon. L. R. LaFLECHE (Minister of National War Services): Since the last sitting of this house I have had the opportunity of reading the official report of the. proceedings of this honourable house. This afternoon I have listened to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and in reply may I say that in the course of my reading I came across certain statements in Hansard attributed to the hon. member. In an effort to understand their position one must have recourse to what

can be found. Among other things I find the following on page 545 of Hansard of June 5, 1940, where the hon. member is reported as having said:
. . . the secret of the recent success of the Germans is the fact that they have consciously planned their economic structure.
And then later on on another occasion he said that the prosperity built up by the socialists was a type of economy which is causing so much trouble today; and also that they did a remarkable job in a short space of time.

I answer this question orally because I would wish, Mr. Speaker, to draw your attention to the kind of question which has been *asked. I have no desire to restrain hon. members from asking questions; on the contrary, I think that they should have full privilege to ask any questions they desire and place them on the order paper. But I do seriously doubt the propriety of placing on the order paper such questions as this. Any one of us, any member of this house and any member of the services, might have some skeleton in his family closet which would be disclosed or to which attention could be drawn by questions of this kind. Personally I think it is not a good practice, and I would hope, Mr. Speaker, that through the Clerk we could find some means whereby at least, when questions of this kind are to be placed on the order paper, the minister and the department concerned would be advised. It so happens in this case that Wing Commander Kennedy is one of the best officers in our service, so that I have no objection to answering the question.

May I, in the absence of the hon. member for York East (Mr. McGregor) who is at the moment out of the chamber, in whose name the question appears on the order paper, say to the minister that while he has made some reference to the kind of question this is, he himself could very readily have spoken to the hon. member and have avoided unnecessary publicity in connection with it.

speakerposition: Associate Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Air; Minister of National Defence for Air and Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I am not the guardian of an hon. member's sense of what is good taste and what is decent. Mr. LaCROIX (Quebec-Montmorency) :/*
1.	Who is the superintendent of dominion government buildings in charge of the distribution of flags which fly over public buildings?
2.	Has this officer a sufficient number of "union jack" flags for public buildings?
3.	When his supply is deficient, does he distribute in lieu thereof "Canadian red ensign" flags?
4.	Has he received an order providing for the replacement of such "Canadian red ensign" flags by "union jack" flags as soon as the stocks of "union jack" flags on order have arrived, with the further instructions that, in the future, only "union jack" flags must fly over public buildings, and that "Canadian red ensign" flags must be used solely for special decoration purposes?
5.	Has the government at last decided to endow Canada with a distinctive national flag so as to replace definitively the "union jack" flag which now flies over all our public buildings ?/
/Mr. MACKENZIE KING: Mr. Speaker, I had better answer this question orally. Section 5 of the question is:
Has the government at last decided to endow Canada with a distinctive national flag so as to replace definitively the "union jack" flag which now flies over all our public buildings?
I would say first of all that the question as worded is neither direct nor straightforward. However the purpose of it is clear enough: it is one which brings up the advisability or inadvisability of creating a flag controversy at a time of war. The question is similar to one which was asked on two occasions, if not on three occasions, at the last session of parliament by the same hon. member. At that time I replied to his question in the following words, on June 21, 1943, as reported in Hansard, pages 3823 and 3824:
A national flag is one which normally is used by a single nation only, and which is used to distinguish that nation from others at international gatherings, and to serve as a symbol of it. The red ensign, with the union jack in the first quarter next to the staff, and the Canadian coat of arms in the fly has for over seventy years been very generally used in situations where a flag specially distinctive of Canada was essential. It was first authorized by the government of Sir John A. Macdonald shortly after confederation for use on Canadian merchant vessels. Its use as a distinctive emblem on all buildings owned or occupied by the Canadian government and situated outside Canada was authorized by order in council on January 26, 1924. It has been popularly accepted as a flag distinctive of Canada.
The union jack, while not a flag distinctive of Canada, may correctly be flown on land in any part of His Majesty's domains.
I question whether this would be a suitable time at which to have parliament determine which particular flag-the union jack, the red ensign, or some other flag to be specially designed-should be declared to be the national flag of Canada.
I have nothing to add to what has been said by the ministry at previous sessions on this matter of a national flag. I should like-however to avail myself of this opportunity to point out that the conference at Quebec in August last presented an occasion on which it was desirable, indeed essential, that a flag specifically distinctive of Canada should be flown. The use of the red ensign flown at the citadel throughout the proceedings of the conference as a symbol of Canada, at the side of the union jack and the stars and stripes, was widely and most favourably commented upon^
The other parts of the hon. member's question are matters of departmental detail which have little or no significance, unless discussion is to be raised on section 5 of the question as asked, and I would request therefore that what I have said be taken as a reply in full.

I explained to the house the other night, when the matter came up, that the inspections referred to are done by the joint inspection board of the United Kingdom and Canada, and that the British government have a substantial interest in the operations of the board because of the fact that only approximately thirty per cent of the inspections are done for the Canadian government. The board reports through me so far as Canada is concerned and through the high commissioner for tl}e United Kingdom so far as the United Kingdom is concerned. I mention this because I have some doubt whether or not reports of this kind, by a board which is conducted as an inspection board and simply as an administrative body set up in this way, should be brought down in this house. I have consulted the high commissioner for the United Kingdom, Mr. MacDonald, and he agrees with me in having no objection in this particular case, save in one respect, and I mention it because it has to do with a general rule that exists in the house. I would not consider it in the public interest to bring down reports made by inspectors to their superiors in connection with this, or any other matter, with which the inspection board is concerned. The house will understand that the inspectors^ are carrying out inspection duties in connection with from
10,000	to 20,000 different items, from boots to guns, radio equipment and so on, and it would be totally irregular and highly prejudicial for the reports of the inspectors to be brought down in connection with these matters. They come within the rule mentioned by the Prime Minister the other day with reference to reports by officers of a department on matters having to do with the department and submitted to a superior officer. Mr. MacDonald and I have no objection to bringing down the correspondence mentioned, that is, the correspondence with the minister but which has not to do with reports made by Mr. Clark at the time he was an employee of the board and acting in his official position as an inspector, these reports being made to his superiors.

speechtext: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee of supply.	* [DOT]

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Before we go into committee of supply, Mr. Speaker, there is a matter I wish to bring to the attention of the house, arising out of the question asked by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) with respect to the floating of a new war loan.
Since the beginning of the war we have raised sums of money beyond anything we dreamed possible before this war started, and that money has been raised through borrowing and taxation. Approximately fifty per cent of the money we have required has been secured through borrowing. I have before me the public accounts for the year 1943, and at page lvii I find these words:
Furthermore, it should be noted that the second victory loan campaign had closed as late as March 7, 1942, hardly more than three weeks before the beginning of the fiscal year 1942-43, and the fourth victory loan drive opened on April 26, 1943, or less than four weeks after the close of the fiscal year. Thus, although only $991-4 million appears as receipts from victory loans during the year ended March 31, 1943, nevertheless in the fifteen months from February 16, 1942, to May 15,	1943, over
$3,143 million in cash was subscribed by the general public in three loan campaigns.
And a little later:
In order to assess the results of the borrowing programme properly, it is necessary to consider
Supply-War Loans

the period from the start of the war to the close of the fiscal year 1942-43, so that accidental factors like the timing of loan campaigns and other transactions will be less important. This is done in table XXIII, which shows that from September 1, 1939, to March 31, 1943, $3,266'8 million out of total new borrowings (that is, excluding the conversion or renewal of previous issues) amounting to $5,124-6 million were subscribed by the general public, or 63-7 per cent.
Since then we have had two more victory loans, the fourth loan for approximately SI,200 million and the fifth loan for something like $1,300 million. So that when you make allowance for the amounts subscribed by the banks, the large insurance companies and various other institutions in Canada, you find that the general public have contributed something over $2,500 million through small individual subscriptions to loans since the beginning of the war.
I should like to see the government give these small investors, who have come forward so willingly, some guarantee that these bonds will not be allowed to fall below par. The large companies, the insurance companies, banks and other institutions holding large blocks of these loans, are quite able to carry them to maturity, when they will receive the par value. The government should give the small investors a guarantee that they also will be able to get par for their bonds.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the policyholders?

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The insurance companies
are quite prepared to carry these bonds to maturity, when they will get 100 cents on the dollar, so that the policyholders are protected. I am speaking in behalf of the thousands of small investors who are to be found in the army, in factories and on farms throughout the country, who have invested in these loans in order to build up savings which may be used for purposes of reestablishment when the war is over.
We all know what took place after the last war. I have a neighbour who served in the army for four years during that war and whose people purchased a $500 war bond for him. In 1920, when he needed money, he sold his bond, but received for it only $450. On the other hand those who were able to carry their bonds to maturity were paid 100 cents cn the dollar, with interest not on $450 but on the full face value of their bonds. I have in my hand the quarterly listings on the Toronto and Montreal stock exchanges for the third victory loan, 5J per cent bonds issued October 27, 1919 and due November 1, 1934, giving the low and high for each quarter. It will be seen that in the quarter ending March 31, 1920,
i A J r. Wright.]
these bonds sold at $97. In December of the same year they sold at a low of 881 and a high of 94. In March, 1921, the low was 92 and the high 96J. In December, 1921, the low was 94J and the high 99J. In 1922 they reached par, and from then until maturity they remained at or above par. As a matter of fact, in March, 1924, the low was 102J and the high 1031, and they went as high as 105J in December of 1927.
Thousands of our soldiers who are overseas are sending home their deferred pay to be put into victory bonds. Thousands of girls in the air force, thousands of workers in factories and thousands of men on the land have subscribed to these bonds. Many of these people will want their money in the period immediately following the war, in order to reestablish themselves, and before another victory loan is floated I think the government should give some assurance that these bonds will be held at par.
I have before me the particulars of the second and third victory loan campaigns in Saskatchewan, and they show that the average subscription was approximately $168 per loan. This indicates that the bonds were bought chiefly by people in the lower income groups. The people who are selling these bonds are telling the farmers to defer their purchases of machinery until after the war and to invest their money in bonds so that when the war is over they will be able to buy the machinery they need. That is the consideration under which a great number of these bonds are being purchased, but unless some further guarantee is given we may again be in the position in which we found ourselves in 1920. At that time certain people in whose interest it was to see that these bonds came down in price were able to bring them down. We should see that that condition does not prevail again and that no profits are made out of the savings of the small purchaser of victory bonds.
It is not enough for the government to say that things are different now, that we have a Bank of Canada which we did not have in 1919 and 1920. It is true that we have a Bank of Canada and that the government have more control over the financial structure of this country than they had at that time, but having that control I think they should give some assurance to the public that they will use it to see that these bonds remain at par. They are the ones who can do this. The people of Canada are willing to contribute and they will contribute if they are given some assurance.
I have a letter from a man who is at present in a sanatorium. He had sold his farm and

Supply-War Loans
wished to invest his money in bonds. He called in a bond salesman and asked if he could guarantee that when, as he anticipated, he left the sanatorium in the course of a couple of years, he would get one hundred cents on the dollar. He was told that if the war continued fdr two or three' years he would get one hundred cents on the dollar, but if the war should end and the old law of supply and demand should again operate and people in the small income groups should sell their bonds in order to reestablish themselves, inevitably the bonds would go below par. As a result, this man did not invest his money in bonds.
I am sure that if the government would come out with a definite statement that these bonds are not to be allowed to go below par, they would find it much easier to float another war loan. I urge upon them that they take this action immediately.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to endorse everything the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) has said, particularly in view of the fact that an insidious campaign is going on in some parts of this country to the effect that should there be a change in government these bonds will not be worth anything. I agree that this government might be changed for a still more reactionary one and then the bonds would be worth much less when the war is over than they are now. That is what will happen if the present economic system remains undirected and uncontrolled in every particular when the war is over.
It seems to me that it would be in the interests of the nation if when we ask for support for the victory loan, particularly from the smaller investors, we make provision for the handling of victory bonds during the first two or three years after the war in such a way that the smaller investor who wants to realize on them to build a home or buy furniture, machinery and so on, will be assured of geting one hundred cents on the dollar. The men and women of Canada who have invested in bonds are entitled to such an assurance. Whenever I have appealed to the people of Canada to put their money into bonds-I shall be glad to do this again as a public duty -I have said to them, and I repeat it to-day, that when they are asked to relinquish their savings for this purpose, especially those who have saved and planned in order to buy bonds because they consider it a patriotic duty, they deserve the guarantee that they will receive one hundred cents on the dollar when they cash them in. I appeal to the Prime Minister and the government to give consideration to this plea.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has said that there is an insidious campaign going on in some parts of the country. May I say to him that in the district from which I come people have been disposing of their bonds, not because there is an insidious campaign by anyone but because of the propaganda of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation that they would take over everything and are against profits. The best guarantee that the people of this country can get that their bonds will be good is to reelect the present government.

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not able on this most unusual occasion to agree with the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). The solution he has in mind is to choose between two evils, and perhaps he regards my hon. friends to the left as the lesser of the two evils.
With regard to the speech just given by my hon. friend to my left, may I saj'' that I regard it as being in the nature of propaganda which has been abroad for some considerable time. What I desire to say to my hon. friends is not by way of supporting the government but rather to refer to a situation which I think ought to be shown up to the people of Canada. The best guarantee we can have that the bonds of Canada will be good after the war is over is to see that we have full employment and maximum production and that the full resources of Canada are put to work. I think it is generally agreed in Canada that that must be done when this war is over. When we have accomplished that-it can be done and it will be done-we shall have answered my hon. friends to my left who are taking the usual defeatist attitude with respect to the whole problem which faces us after the war is over. They talk about rationing scarcity and guaranteeing minimums, but our job is to see that maximums are provided for the people of Canada. If the proper course is followed, not only will the bondholders be guaranteed a minimum of one dollar for each dollar invested, but I am hopeful that with the increase of opportunities and prosperity in Canada the men and women who hold these bonds will receive a premium on every one of them. We have no right as Canadian citizens to think that any other condition will exist when this war is over.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) has made out a good case for the point he raised. We have had a nice propagandist speech by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon). It is always said that this group
Supply-War Loans

is carrying on propaganda, but during the present session the leader of the opposition has never risen in his place without making a propagandist speech. I wish to say to him that there is no use in telling the people of Canada what is going to happen when this war is over.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The C.C.F. has been doing it right along.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Wait until I finish. The people of Canada know what you did after the last war. The people of Canada know the promise made in 1930 by the leader of the Conservative party.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are promising now.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Wait a minute. He said: We will end unemployment or perish in the attempt. They perished. They perished because they tried to end unemployment under the system that created unemployment. Because they were going to end unemployment in that way, they perished. We are making no bones about it. We are learning that unemployment cannot be ended under the present system. The only way you can end unemployment under capitalism is by making a war. You ended unemployment between 1914 . and 1918, but you had unemployment again as soon as the war was over and you had it almost continuously from then on until the present war began.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh no.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The facts are against my hon. friend. Possibly he was not unemployed. But was there not unemployment between 1929 and 1939?

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, but was there not unemployment between 1922 and 1929?

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, lots of it. Ask those who were in office at the time. Perhaps my hon. friend has never heard about the famous five-cent piece speech.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We heard about it.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That incident arose at a time when the provinces needed assistance because of unemployment and other conditions and the federal government of the day was not prepared to give it to them.
The question the member for Melfort raised is this. We are asking the people of this country to invest their savings in bonds- invest, remember. It may be that we shall be met within a short time with the conditions that prevailed in the thirties, or yes, in the twenties. The price of bonds may fall and as prices fall people will rush to dispose of their bonds. What we are asking is this: since the
[Mr. MacJnnin.l
government will pay one hundred cents on the dollar on these bonds at maturity, there is no reason in the world why they should not give the assurance now that they will protect the small investor by paying one hundred cents on the dollar if he has to dispose of his bonds at any time before maturity. It would not cost the government of this country anything, because when the bonds mature they will pay them off at one hundred cents on the dollar anyway. I am satisfied that the member for Melfort has raised a pertinent and important question, not one that should be met with sneers and hilarity in this house. People who have at heart the interests of the working man and the working woman-small investors-should realize that once they lose their jobs they are only two or three weeks away from the breadline. These are the people we should protect.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The hon. member has no monopoly of interest in the working man to make him his champion.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe the raising of this question in the house is timely. It is fitting that we should call on the leader of the opposition (Mr. Graydon) to tell the house at the earliest opportunity how the Progressive Conservatives, if they came into power, would maintain total use and total employment. In the light of the tragic failure of the Conservatives between 1930 and 1935, they need to show just in what respects they have changed their policy to guarantee total use and total employment. It is utter nonsense talking about what they are going to do unless they show how that intention is to be realized.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We have not the same winter as we had last year, have we?

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
No, but you have a whole lot of the same brains in the Conservative party, and thus far I have not seen any evidence of any different brains or of any different use of the old brains. I think the real problem which the Liberals have is to show the house and the people that they really do know how to manage the economy of this country so that they can maintain the value of its bonds at par. The problem which faces the C.C.F. is not so much to raise questions like this as it is to show the country that they know how to manage the economy of the country. We hear much talk about its being necessary only to change the system in order to achieve total employment and total use. I agree with that. But the change must be the correct change. When the C.C.F. succeed in showing us how merely

Supply-War Loans
changing to government ownership of industry is going to guarantee the total use of Canada'6 natural resources and the total employment of Canada's people, that party will be in a far stronger position.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), with whom I have no particular quarrel, has asserted that so long as capitalism continues it will be impossible to achieve total use and total employment. I point out that the all-important thing is to provide markets internally. If purchasing power can be supplied to the people to enable them to buy a sufficient amount of the products that industry stands ready to turn out, we shall be able to employ at home, our full resources, both human and material. Until that is done, it will matter not who owns the industries. I do believe it. would be an excellent thing for this house to take a few hours off, several times before the end of this session, to canvass with the greatest of care and examine with the most minute scrupulousness just exactly what we need to do to be able to guarantee security after the war is over.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the best guarantee we can have that the country's bonds will maintain their value is a guarantee that the national income will be maintained at its present level. When that is done there will be no need for people to sell their bonds because then they will be receiving wages to enable them to maintain a decent standard of living. If it is the intention of the government that the national income shall be maintained at its present level, I do not think anybody would suggest that it is not within the power of the government to secure that. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), on the declaration of war, said that no financial restrictions would be allowed to impede the war effort. Is the Prime Minister prepared to make a declaration that no financial restrictions will be allowed to impede our peace-time effort, and that the only limits to the national income will be the ability of the people to produce in order to maintain the national income? I think it would be a very good thing for the country at large if at this time the Prime Minister in no uncertain way would declare that no financial restrictions are to be allowed to impede the success of the post war era; that whatever money is required to maintain the fullest development of our resources will be. forthcoming.
There is a reason why there is fear in people's minds, and it is this. When Doctor James was speaking before the senate he said
that after the war we would have to adopt a new budget philosophy. He said we might have to be prepared to increase the national debt every year for the next hundred years. The only exception I take to that statement is this: why say a hundred years? Why not be frank and say that as long as we are operating under this system the national debt will hhve to increase for ever?
On the other hand the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has taken a different stand. He brought in a return last year in which he stated that the national debt could be paid off, and that the government would probably introduce a scientific scheme under which the national debt would be paid. What does that mean? If we are going to introduce a scientific scheme to pay off the national debt, you must have not only a balanced budget but a budget with a surplus in order to pay off the debt. There you have the adviser on reconstruction saying that you are going to increase your national debt every year for a hundred years, while on the other hand the Minister of Finance is saying that you are not going to increase your national debt, but that you are going to have a budget surplus and pay off your national debt.
I think we all realize that if we are to have again a period similar to that from 1935 to 1939, when vre had a minister of finance who deliberately set himself to curtail expenses in order to have a balanced budget, very soon after the war we shall go back into the depths of depression, destroy the confidence of the people, and have unemployment increasing. If unemployment increases, people who hold small bonds w-ill start to cash them, and the minute they begin to do so the value will depreciate. It is high time that we had a declaration from the Prime Minister assuring this country that whatever money is necessary to develop to the fullest extent the resources of this country after the war will be forthcoming.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had thought during the period since war was declared, those in a minority like myself who hold strong views on certain reforms would be well advised to defer the pushing of them forward until the greater and more immediate task of defeating the enemy should be accomplished. I have been accused on a good many occasions of failing to follow the course of reform which started before the banking and commerce committee of 1934, and which at times I am afraid I followed a little too vigorously, until the Bank of Canada became a publicly owned, nationally administered institution. That was a great step
Supply-War Loans

towards finding solutions of all of our supply-problems, but I still believe that we have to go much farther and nationalize the policy of the Bank of Canada; change it from a filling station to the chartered banks into an institution of national service that will truly accomplish the purpose of issuing national currency and national credit in terms of public need and not in terms of private gain.
I rise, Mr. Speaker, solely for the purpose of drawing to the attention of my colleagues in this house a document which I believe is probably the most significant and far-reaching that has been published in Canada this year. It is the report for 1943 of the governor of the Bank of Canada. I believe it is important because, if you will take the time to read the preamble of the Bank of Canada Act, you will find that it is established as a public utility charged with the responsibility of sustaining and advancing and expanding and regulating the economic life of the government and the people of this nation. Now, what Mr. Towers has to say, from the position which he holds and the access which he alone has to the information available, should make any pronouncement by him one of the utmost importance not only to parliament but to everyone in the dominion. Let me deal with just one or two of these statements.
At page 5 you will find a statement of the change in our national debt situation. He points out that our national debt from August 31, 1939, has risen from $4,693,000,000 to $11,-
302,000,000 on December 1, 1943. That is the federal debt only. It shows an increase of $6,609,000,000, and carries with it an increase in interest charges from S169,000,000 to $304,000,000 a year. Later in the report Mr. Towers attempts to sweeten that interest charge of $304,000,000 by pointing out that we might consider it reduced by offsetting the earnings of the foreign exchange control board, earnings of the Bank of Canada, and earnings of such institutions as our national harbours. But no matter what you set off against it, the fact is that the interest charge has been increased to $304,000,000 a year, which means that over the next decade the taxpayers including the men who are fighting and the men who are working to win this war and the youth of to-day must find $3,040,000,000 for interest charges alone.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In a decade, I said. Yes, if people would think in terms of tens of years when they think of interest they would probably be more concerned about its ultimate consequences.

What does Mr. Towers say about that debt situation? On page 11 of the report he says:
I do not wish to suggest that public debt could be increased at the present rate for an indefinite period without placing intolerable strain on our economy. I do feel, however, that the war debt, and the increases which will inevitably take place for a time after the war ends, can be handled without serious embarrassment.
Neither Mr. Towers nor any other man alive to-day can tell when this war is going to end or what the ultimate cost may be. I believe we have every reason to be confident that victory is certain. Certainly the war power of Germany is declining, while the war power of the united nations is steadily advancing. But no one can be certain as to when Germany can be brought to unconditional surrender, if this war is to be prosecuted with a due regard for the unnecessary sacrifice of the lives and the suffering of the men in our own fighting forces. I believe that in the Pacific the Americans are successfully achieving what the Germans hoped and failed to do to the British isles. I believe that slowly but surely the American fleet and air power of the Pacific are destroying the lines of sea transport of the Japanese people, without which the Japanese cannot survive. But again no one can tell how soon or at what cost that end can be finally achieved. Certainly as we look at the future we know that this war is not going to end with an armistice and treaties of peace. On the contrary, it is going to end with armies of occupation. Reparations are not in the offing. The reestablishment and maintenance of order and the reconstruction of a world that has been bathed in the flames of devastation are to be a part of the cost of victory. How then can the governor of the Bank of Canada give any assurance that a debt unknown can be carried without embarrassment? Already the debt load of this war is placing an intolerable strain upon the economy of the nation.
There is one other feature in connection with that phase of our reconstruction that we all should keep in mind, and that is that during the last war there were accumulations of cash reserve. We have imposed a policy of taxation during this war deliberately designed to take away from the people, from business organizations, all forms of profit. That too will place a heavier strain upon the exchequer of national, provincial and municipal governments in the reconstruction period.
In addition to that, our municipalities and provinces, with their limited revenues, although they have some reserves accumulated from deferred maintenance and income from war

Supply-War Loans
expenditures, are not in as good a position to expand their debts as they were after the last war ended. What does Mr. Towers say about all this? He reviews, as every man who thinks on the subject at all must do, the problems of demobilization and reconstruction. The men and the women to be demobilized from our fighting forces are not of the same type that came back from the last war. Our air force is made up very largely, if not almost entirely, in the flying forces, of men of the officer and non-commissioned officer class, and the ground forces are men who are highly-trained and highly-skilled artisans and mechanics. In our navy the same problem, probably not so intense, is to be found, while our armed forces are men largely trained in the skill of operating highly mechanized organizations. All these forces have had their standards of living in the service greatly raised above what they were during the last war. It is not going to be as easy to find the kind of employment that will be acceptable to them as it was at the end of the last war, and the problem is infinitely greater.
We have also the problem of an industrial army who have found the highest standards of pay and the best working conditions in the most modern factories. Hundreds of thousands of them will not only be looking for employment of a similar kind but will be unhappy if they have to move down into some category of employment that is inferior. Therefore when Mr. Towers says that we can look forward to carrying our war debt and the postwar costs and costs of reconstruction without embarrassment and without placing an intolerable strain upon the economy of our nation, he is moving in the realm not of factual statement but of purely theoretical speculation. Mr. Towers, however, takes that situation and leaves it upon the doorstep of the government, upon the doorstep of parliament, because in his conclusion this is what he says:
The adjustments required will clearly be of unprecedented magnitude, and bold planning on the part of labour, farm and business organizations as well as the governments is urgently needed.
Now when the governor of the Bank of Canada tells this government and this parliament and the people of the Dominion of Canada that they face adjustments of unprecedented magnitude and that bold planning is urgently required, be makes a statement which I believe we in this House of Commons cannot ignore and should not delay in acting upon.
I do not want to be a defeatist, although I may say that I do heartily subscribe to the proposition that a fair price of our bonds should be fixed and that Canadians, many of 100-60
whom, out of a pure spirit of patriotism, accumulated their savings in the form of bonds, should not be the victims of the discount market when the war ends. If the government can limit the ceiling of a man's wages the government ought to be able to guarantee him against a loss of his investment in our national securities.
There is one other thing to which I would call the attention of members of the house and of my colleagues, and that is the method of financing which we have developed, because I believe that, in owning the Bank of Canada, we have demonstrated that we have an institution of inestimable value, already proven, and one which can prove of even greater value in the difficult days that lie ahead. Yes, there are difficult days ahead, not impossible, but they are going to require the best of economic understanding, good judgment and statesmanship to see us through.
Mr. Towers at page 6 says that during 1943, Canadian deposit liabilities of the chartered banks increased by 8748,000,000. That was new money created by the chartered banks by merely writing up bank deposit entries in their books and exchanging them for interestbearing bonds. Now he says:
Total active note circulation, including Bank of Canada notes, rose by $161,000,000. making the total expansion in the volume of money, therefore, $909,000,000.
And he goes on to review some of the things the banks have acquired in the way of government securities, but he does not give us a' clear statement of what has been purchased by the chartered banks of Canada. However, he comes along with this statement:
"Cash reserves of the chartered hanks rose $82,000,000 during the year, as shown in the table on page 1. Most of the expansion was necessary in order to maintain the cash ratio position of the chartered banks in view of the $748,000,000 increase in their Canadian deposit liabilities referred to above."
What does that mean? I believe it means that the Bank of Canada has issued into circulation, which circulation eventually came into the possession of the chartared banks, $82,000,000 of Bank of Canada legal tender bills. With that $82,000,000 the banks were able to increase their deposits up to
5520.000.	000 and did increase them up to
5748.000.	000. You see what is happening. Here we have a national banking institution owned by the people of Canada, issuing Canadian legal tender as a cold subsidy to our chartered banks, and with that subsidy of cash, which is the biggest subsidy any monopoly ever received, they are manufacturing in their own books the means of buying Canadian government interest bearing bonds. Was there ever such a device and system devised and sus-

Supply-War Loans

tained by sane men for the wreck of government and the benefit of private enterprise? There you have the meaning-at least what I always thought was the meaning-of issuing currency and credit in terms of private gain. That is the fundamental basis of our whole banking system that must be changed before government, which has the constitutional right and power and responsibility of issuing currency, can move along the fields of solvency and away from the bankruptcy that this false debt claim system will continue to impose upon us.	.
We have seen the tragedy in the republic to the south of us in the last few days. We have seen a president guided by the experts of the treasury board finding upon his hands at this critical period the greatest revolt of the Congress of the United States against bureaucracy and against oligarchy that has ever been recorded. President Roosevelt is the victim of the same bad advice, the same unfortunate advice, that brought Winston Churchill to disaster when he was Chancellor of the British Exchequer from 1925 to 1929. Standing on the floor of the House of Commons in 1932 and 1936, he pointed out that he took full responsibility for the tragedies that had occurred during that period; but he said that he had acted upon the advice of the monetary experts of England, who had assured him that in the policies they proposed they were returning to reality and stability. Yes, Churchill, in his happy ability to acknowledge an error when he makes it, said: "I made a mistake. I was the last of the orthodox chancellors of the exchequer. Look upon me as the last of the Mohicans." When that kind of thing goes on disaster is certain to follow, and if we as a Liberal government find ourselves out of tune with the people of Canada to-day, it is the encroachment of financial authority over administrative responsibility that is shaking the confidence of the people not in our ability to win the war, but in our ability to sustain full employment at any other time than when we are fighting a war.	[DOT]
I hope this document, of the Bank of Canada report, will be considered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) as a document that should go at once to the banking and commerce committee; because if the governor of the Bank of Canada can warn the government of Canada, the Canadian parliament and the people of Canada that he finds that adjustments of unprecedented magnitude are required and that bold planning is urgently needed, we should have at the service of this parliament and the government all the information that Mr. Towers has to justify that statement.
[Mr. McGeer.l
Let me say to you that all the good work the committee on war expenditures is doing- it is saving a few million dollars-comes to naught when you remember that all the while the whole nation is engaged in war this false system is mulcting the nation not in millions, but in billions of dollars. No government can survive, no minister of finance can carry on under this system, and the sooner we come to a realization of what we meant in 1935 when we said we would establish a Bank of Canada and give it power, and see that the powers were enforced, to issue currency and credit in terms of public need, the better. I believe that we are close to the day when that will come about; when instead of lending our medium of exchange through the debt claim system, we shall be spending the medium of exchange required to sustain the economy of the nation in balanced proportions, free from the debt system. Then, Mr. Speaker, we shall find that debt, unpayable debt, will cease to bind the health and the freedom of the people.

speechtext: I have just two points to lay before the house in the discussion now proceeding. speechtext: But you people are trying an altogether new system now.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Let me tell my hon. friend that it has done an immense amount of good. It has gone very far in economic reform, and it can go a step further according to my philosophy of banking. I support the request of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, which I feel sure will be granted, that this splendid report of Mr. Graham Towers, the governor of the Bank of Canada, dated February 10, 1944, be forthwith referred to the banking and commerce committee, so that all parties may participate in that committee and endeavour to make provision, as Mr. Towers asks us to do, for the adjustment required which will "clearly be of unprecedented magnitude and bold planning." No one can begin to plan for the future until after making adjustments which have to do with economic policy. Everyone can see that our bold planning for the future, no matter by what party it may be done nor on what particular lines it may be advocated, in the last analysis depends upon the economic system which is the foundation of our ability to employ people and to create trade relations which will deal with our surpluses, and which in fact is at the very root of our national welfare. If that be so, Mr. Speaker, let us get to work on this important problem with as little delay as possible.
I should like to deal with one other point. Let me say at once that I am wholly in favour of the suggestion that the government should guarantee the outstanding bonds at par, so that investors may not suffer loss as a result of their patriotic and saving-minded purchases of these bonds, at the instance of all of us. But let me address a word to the complaint which the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party (Mr. Coldwell) put on record in his opening remarks. If I understood him aright he voiced the complaint that there were invidious rumours afloat-

speechtext:
"Insidious" was the
word I used.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well, perhaps "invidious" will pretty well describe the idea he wanted to convey to the people of Canada. He said there were invidious rumours afloat as to what would occur if the C.C.F. party took office. By that I suppose he meant rumours which cast doubt upon the ability of his administration, if he ever got to the point of forming one, and upon the value of our good Canadian bonds outstanding, now total-' ling about $8,000 million, if his party came to power. Let me make clear to him that the unrest growing in a great many quarters, not only in this country but also in the United States, as to the possibility of his party gaining power in this country, is due in large part, in my judgment, to the hon. member having gone to the United States and there making a speech or speeches which received a good deal of publicity. I am not sure whether the speech was broadcast, but I think it was delivered, in New York or Washington, or perhaps in both cities. At any rate he assured the 130,000,000 people of that great republic that he thought he saw the rising of the sun and believed there was a prospect of his party taking over the government of the Dominion of Canada in the near future, or something to that effect; I hope I have paraphrased with reasonable accuracy the statement made by my hon. friend. He also told his audience, in part at least, that the first thing his party would do when they came to power would be to nationalize the banks of Canada. To nationalize the banks means to politicalize them; that is, the ten commercial banks doing business with the public in Canada.

speechtext: How about the Bank of Canada? Is it politicalized?

The Bank of Canada is a national bank in the true sense; as my hon. friend well knows, it is without power or

authority to lead money to him or to his colleagues or to any other individual or corporation in this country. maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Bank of Canada lends money to the private banks, and the private banks lend it to us.

maintopic: WAR LOANS-STATEMENT OF MR. WRIGHT ON MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: All right; the private banks lend it to individuals. By his timely interruption the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy) has emphasized the very point I am going to make. I said that the C.C.F. policy of nationalizing the private commercial banks of the country means to politicalize them; and to politicalize them as understood by my hon. friends-the hon. member for York South is very keen about it-means to "C.C.F-erize" them, nothing more or less. Let us try to visualize the picture my hon. friend painted to the people of the United States. If by chance he should come to power in Canada his first act-I think it has been placed first and foremost-would be to lock the doors of the ten chartered banks of Canada. Probably then we would find standing outside the door of one of our banks, in blue uniforms with brass buttons, the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) and his absent colleague the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr Gillis), saying, "How do you do, Mr. Customer; come in. How much would you like? What can we lend you to-day?" Oh, what a picture! A modest fellow, perhaps from up my way, would come along and say, "I am one of a group of eight or ten. We have got $10,000 together and we would like another $10,000 with which to set up a plant to cut pulpwood to be sold to the railway." I can visualize one of these two hon. gentlemen, resplendent in his uniform, saying, "Well, that is very nice of you. We want to encourage enterprise, but do you belong to the C.C.F.?" has some wonderful ideas. Then come back to-morrow and bring your membership card, and we shall be very happy indeed to reconsider your application for a loan of $10,000 to open up Canadian industry."
Mr. MacINNIS They do that in connection with the roads now; so why not in connection with the banks? You cannot get a job on the roads in British Columbia without a membership card in the Liberal party.

One does not need to search outside the pamphlets of the C.C.F. for the source of the rumours that have been going about western Canada to the effect that if the C.C.F. party got into power in this country they would see to it that the victory bonds-and the greater the bond the greater the discount-would be discounted. Further, we feel that to make this definite guarantee at this time would not only encourage people in the purchasing of victory bonds but would help to convince them that we in, this house are sure there will be maintenance of full employment after the war is over. On the other hand, in view of the experience of the period after the last war, when war bonds went down in value with the result that financial and investment houses profited from the situation, people cannot help feeling that the refusal to make such a commitment at the present time is simply a case of leaving the door open for the same thing to happen again if the value of these bonds does go down.
I come back to the statement I made a moment ago, that if the leader of the opposition and if the Minister of Agriculture and other members of the government are so confident that our economy will be at a high level after the war, no loss will be involved in making this commitment and we feel definitely that it should be made. We urge that not only because there will be no loss, but because of the assurance that it would give to our people. I would point out that the Minister of Agriculture-again in a vigorous and interesting speech-wandered all over the field but did not deal with the specific request which the hon. member for Melfort has brought to thp attention of this house. I hope that some other minister speaking on behalf of the government will even yet rise and give this assurance to the house and to the country. The

matter was raised quite sincerely and in a straightforward manner by the hon. member for Melfort. We feel that this is something concerning which the people of Canada deserve to be given assurance, and we deplore the way in which the issue has been side-tracked, the way in which many hon. members have wandered all over the field, the way in which no real answer has been given to this question.
I should like to say a word about the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture in connection with certain literature which he had in his hand a moment ago. I do not happen to have a copy before me, but I should like to point out that we are proposing that steps should be taken now, so as to avoid the necessity of doing what in 1933 our people in Saskatchewan felt it was necessary to do. What happened then was that victory bonds from the last war had got out of the hands of the small holders; they had taken a loss, and the bonds were now in the hands of a few holders. The C.C.F. people, or our predecessors, whoever drafted the material which the ^Minister of Agriculture has in his hands, felt that it was high time that the profits which a few people had made at that time should be brought to a halt; and it is our contention that we should avoid that kind of a situation arising again, by making it clear now that the victory bonds which people are purchasing in this war will not deteriorate in value so far as the small purchasers are concerned. It has already been pointed out that since the government guarantees the value of these bonds at maturity, and we emphasize that point, there is no loss to be incurred by the government in guaranteeing the value of the bonds at all times. That may raise in someone's mind the obvious question: if there is no loss to the government, why is there so much opposition to our request? The answer is that if the stand we are asking for is taken by the government it will shut the door to many financial and investment houses, against the making of huge profits from the buying of these bonds if they depreciate in value after the war. We feel that this is a step that should be taken. After all, these are the savings of the people, given for the specific purpose of victory, given also with the suggestion that they might have this money on hand for rehabilitation purposes after the war. We feel, therefore, that our people should not be exploited by leaving the door open in this way to financial and' investment houses.
I have done what I could to bring the discussion back to the request which the hon. member for Melfort submitted to the house, which we feel is a reasonable one and which

I regret the unavoidable absence at the moment of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley), and on his behalf I should like to make a few observations. The question raised by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) is not a new question. The hon. member for Yorlcton (Mr. Castleden) raised it last year and the minister answered him fully at that time. I have no doubt the question will come up again.
What we should bear in mind is this. The hon. member for Melfort asks that the government should guarantee every holder of a victory bond that he will be able at any time to sell that bond for 100 cents on the dollar.
I suggest that we should remember what the government does when it issues bonds. It is issuing bonds for five, ten and fifteen years, paying a certain rate of interest in consideration of the fact that the money is lent for that term. It guarantees that at maturity of that term the holder will receive 100 cents on the dollar.
I do not intend to go into the pros and cons of the hon. gentleman's suggestion except to say that if that suggestion were accepted it would mean that there would be no difference between the rate of interest which the government would pay for thirty days or sixty days and the rate on money which it might borrow for ten, fifteen or twenty years.
As I say, this question has been fully discussed before. The Minister of Finance gave a full explanation as to why the government could not agree with the suggestion made by the hon. member for Yorkton last year, and I would not think his views would have changed in the meantime.
So much for the suggestion that the government should now guarantee the holder of every bond 100 cents on the dollar at any time. Perhaps we are taking too much for granted in assuming that the holder will not get it. A good many of these bonds now sell at a premium. They are widely distributed among a large number of small holders, far more than ever before, and I believe that the very fact of that wide distribution will make for stability in the price of these bonds on the open market during and after the war.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to take this opportunity to make a statement in regard to mail to troops overseas.
During the past six or eight weeks I have received a number of letters complaining of delay and non-delivery of mails to and from members of the Canadian armed forces overseas. Items and editorials have also appeared in the daily press.
In dealing with this matter, I can assure you that I have a sympathetic appreciation and understanding of the anxiety of parents, relatives and friends, in this country when they fail to receive news from overseas or when they hear that the letters and parcels which they have sent overseas have not arrived.
Knowing how important the receipt of mail is from a standpoint of morale, I can assure you that, despite delays which have occurred, advantage has been, and will be taken, of every means at our disposal to improve the service.
That there have been delays there is no doubt, but not delays which could be avoided. The time taken, which to anxious relatives and friends may seem unreasonable, is due to three more or less unavoidable causes:-
(1)	the lack of transport, both air and surface, on account of the imperative and incessant requirements for vital operations,
(2)	adverse transatlantic weather usually prevalent in the winter months,
(3)	the necessary movement of personnel from unit to unit and location to location to meet the exigencies of active operations.
Last fall there were indications that shipping space for the transportation of mails overseas was becoming more difficult to obtain as some of the larger ships which had been used were being moved from the Canadian route for other purposes.
We had counted on being able to overtake this difficulty by the transmission of a large portion of the letter mails from Canada to the United Kingdom by air. Unfortunately, the aircraft which we had hoped would be available did not materialize due to the prior demands of machines for combat purposes.
On October 7 a meeting took place between the Minister of National Defence, the minister for air and myself, together with representatives of the Post Office Department and the Canadian armed forces postal services.

Supply-Post Office
As a result of personal representations made by the Minister of National Defence for Air, six Fortress aircraft were obtained from the United States to be utilized for the transportation of mails for the forces. These machines were not new but had been used in varying ' degrees for operation and training purposes.
A Royal Canadian Air Force squadron was created to operate the mail service from Canada to the United Kingdom and on to the Mediterranean area, and return.
I should like to make it clear at this point that this service was supplementary to the facilities which existed, and despite deiays which have occurred the fact emerges that this Canadian air service has carried to the United Kingdom and the Mediterranean theatre, and return, thousands of pounds of letters which would otherwise have been dispatched by surface ships.
An air service of this nature would ordinarily not have been inaugurated without an extended period of experimental flights to seek out the handicaps and difficulties and apply the remedies before the actual service flights commenced.
In our desire to take advantage of every possible means of expediting delivery, it' was decided to commence the service without these usual tests and to iron out the difficulties as we went along. This we have done. Difficulties have been encountered, many of them, but I believe that I can confidently say that most of these difficulties are now behind us and that, with a reasonable break in the weather, noticeable improvements will be effected.
It must, however, be borne in mind that war-time transport cannot be compared with that enjoyed in peace times. The handicaps and the obstacles are many. Delays will occur, due chiefly to the exigencies of war. We shall, however, continue, as we have in the past, to overlook no opportunity and to take advantage of every facility to improve the service to the men and women serving overseas.
So that you will have some idea of the reasons for the delays which have occurred and the average times which it takes to handle and transport mails from Canada to the overseas forces under present conditions, I am going to place on record data taken from actual mail service operations from Canada to the United Kingdom and the Mediterranean theatre. Air letters and airgraphs from the United Kingdom to the Mediterranean theatre were formerly carried on any aircraft on which there was available space. Usually the planes of the RA.F. transport command and the United States transport command were used. Recently the mails have been carried by the R.C.A.F. transport command, and nine round trips have been made since the first trip which left the United Kingdom on Christmas Day, 1943. As a result of the experience gained through the initial trips it was decided, in addition to the present equipment, to base a lighter type of transport aircraft at a western Mediterranean airport. This will permit a round trip service to the Mediterranean circuit every five days and oft.ener if the quantity of mail justifies. It is confidently expected that this will reduce the elapsed time by several days. The first of these planes has already arrived at the airport and the improved service will go into operation in the very near future. With the advent of improved weather the delays will be further reduced by possibly two or three days and, as the lighter aircraft will be able to land closer to the point where the postal base is located, time now taken up by extended road transport will be eliminated.
Changes of this kind, however, are not effected overnight. They are the result of many negotiations and preliminaries. First, planes must be obtained, having regard to the needs of combat operations and, further, aircraft cannot go rushing into zones of operations without previous measures being taken in regard to control, security and navigation. That this improved service is now ready to operate speaks for itself. I conservatively estimate that in a short while it will effect a saving in time of up to ten days between Canada and the Mediterranean theatre, weather permitting.

During the eight weeks since the R.C.A.F. service has been in operation, 45,619 pounds of mail, approximately two and a quarter million letters, have been carried by air from England to the Mediterranean theatre. This has reduced the time of delivery in some cases by almost two weeks.

Times given are for normal items addressed to definite units. The time is appreciably increased when the mail is intended for reinforcement units or for personnel who have been routed through reinforcement depots to definite units. In such cases, the mail has to pass through the postal tracing section, sometimes on two or three different occasions, and the time required is increased accordingly.
It happens from time to time that when these mails are dispatched by surface ships the ships are re-routed to a different port from that originally intended. This further complicates the mail handling and increases the time for delivery. In addition, several incidents have occurred when ships have been damaged and have had to put back to port. On other occasions they have had to enter a port en route for repairs.
At the time of the first expedition of Canadian forces to the Mediterranean area mails were frozen in the United Kingdom until the troops were well on their way to destination. This action was taken by the security authorities in the interests of the safety of the convoy. Unfortunately when the mails were eventually dispatched one of the ships carrying them was damaged by enemy action which necessitated it putting into port for repairs. This took a considerable time and created still further delay.

During the year 1943, twenty-seven and a half million pounds of parcel post were dispatched overseas from Canada. This represents 6,930,835 parcels. Of this number 3,008,969 were tobacco parcels which are each individually listed by the Canadian postal corps before dispatch.
As far as possible parcels are shipped in direct unit bags, which means that the bag containing the parcels and the corresponding list is sealed at the base post office, Canada, and the seals are intact when delivered to the post orderly of the unit overseas. When it is not practical to sort tobacco parcels into unit bags, the consolidation takes place at the Canadian overseas postal depot in the United Kingdom where the individual tobacco parcels are checked in and again listed on being dispatched to the units.
During 1943 losses by enemy action decreased sharply, and it is estimated that losses from all causes are only slightly more than 1 per cent while the mails are in the custody of the Canadian armed forces postal service. Losses do occur when parcels are in custody of the British postal service or after delivery to the units. The Cana'dian postal corps endeavours to reduce these losses as far as possible by inspection of the unit mail rooms. There is, however, a limit as to what can be done in this connection.
In most cases of complaints concerning cigarette parcels cognizance is not taken of the time actually required for a parcel to reach its destination even under favourable conditions. Representations of non-delivery are made before the parcel has had time to reach its destination. Time and again investigation has shown that the parcels complained about were delivered in the normal course of time.
It should be borne in mind that delays also occur between the time an order is placed at the corner tobacconist and the time it is received by the tobacco company, also between the time the order is received by the tobacco company and the date it is delivered to the Canadian postal corps for handling and dispatch.
Many parcels are received which are inadequately addressed. This is sometimes due to misreading of the written address when the address label is typed. Search after search is made through records in an endeavour to locate the correct addressee.
When a parcel finally fails of delivery it is turned over to the auxiliary services of the Canadian armed forces for distribution generally to Canadian armed forces personnel. In all cases where this action is taken a letter is sent to the sender advising him of the treatment given to the parcel.

During the months of November, December and January 621,440 parcels were dispatched from the United Kingdom to the central Mediterranean.
The majority of these were Christmas parcels from Canada, and it is estimated that the bulk would reach Italy some time during January.
All parcel mails do not travel from Canada to the Mediterranean via the United Kingdom. Arrangements were made in the fall of the year with the United States army postal authorities whereby Canadian mails could be dispatched through United States ports. It was provided by the United States authorities, however, that this arrangement could only take effect after their Christmas bulk had been cleared.
A number of dispatches have already been made via United States ports and it is estimated that the average transit time from the base post office in Canada to Italy is approximately fifty days. Occasionally, however, these steamers are diverted to a port other than the original destination. This generally

Our chief concern in connection with mails to Italy centres in items addressed to the personnel of reinforcement units. The difficulty eases once they have been posted to definite units, but while the men are moving from a reinforcement unit in England to a reinforcement group and depots in Italy and from one reinforcement battalion to another reinforcement battalion and then eventually to a definite unit, the possibility of expeditious handling is remote.
Items have to be routed through the records several times before the addressee is located, and often by the time the parcel reaches that location he has moved on to some other point. This difficulty is not peculiar to the Canadian army. It is met with in all forces.
Eventually the mail catches up with the addressee, and two incidents have very recently come to my attention where men had moved from one unit to another or from one location to another. One man received 107 items at one time, and another seventy-eight.
In an endeavour to give a picture of this situation I propose to read a statement of the channels through which the mails would pass in connection with reinforcement units. In case the impression might prevail that this is a hypothetical statement, I am taking the liberty of reading a letter which I have just received:
February 21, 1914.
The Postmaster General,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Sir:
I wish to bring to your attention a situation which, if possible, should be remedied.
My son was wounded on December 19, while serving with the West Nova Scotia regiment. His Christmas parcels were mailed before November 1, securely packed and tied and properly addressed. These parcels were addressed to him at 7 C.I.R.U. England, but he had moved to the 1st Battalion 1 C.B.R.D. in North Africa. Later he moved to the 4th Battalion 1 C.B.R.D. which station, I believe, is in Italy.
The young man wrote me under date of January 29 that he had not received a letter or a parcel since the middle of October. Since November, the family have sent him several parcels and letters, some addressed to North Africa and the balance to the 4th Battalion 1 C.B.R.D.
I know you will appreciate that it is discouraging to both the young man and his family, that his parcels and letters are not being received.
Yours very truly,
Perhaps I might be allowed to put on Hansard, as it covers two-and-a-half typewritten pages, a description of the travel of a letter addressed to a member of a reinforcement unit recently arrived in the United Kingdom who is included in a draft for the Mediterranean theatre.
