Brief description of the travel of a letter addressed to a member of a reinforcement unit recently arrived in the United Kingdom who is included in a draft for the Mediterranean theatre.
Letter is forwarded from Canada in the usual way, addressed to a reinforcement unit in England. Time required, air mail approximately ten days, surface mail approximately thirty days.
Letter arrived in the United Kingdom but there is yet no record at the reinforcement unit of the addressee.
Letter is then forwarded to the Canadian records in England and search made for the addressee's correct address.
Often there is no trace in records as the information is not yet complete concerning the unit to which the addressee has been posted.
The letter is held for a week and then put through Canadian records again.
If records contain information of unit to which the addressee is posted, letter is endorsed accordingly.
If there is still no record of addressee, the letter is held another week and is put through the Canadian records again at regular intervals until he is found.
The redirected letter is forwarded to the Canadian overseas postal depot, England, for sortation and dispatch.
The letter arrives at the reinforcement unit in England to which the addressee has been posted. It is sorted to the respective company by the unit mail orderly.
Letter is delivered to the addressee if he is still in the United Kingdom.
If the addressee has been included in a reinforcement draft for the Mediterranean theatre the letter is so endorsed by- the unit mail orderly.
Letter is forwarded, from the reinforcement unit in the United Kingdom to the Canadian overseas postal depot for sortation and dispatch to the Mediterranean theatre.
Letter is forwarded to the reinforcement depot, central Mediterranean force, time required approximately thirty days by surface, six to sixteen days by air.
Letter arrives at base post office, Mediterranean theatre, and dispatched to the postal tracing section, Canadian 2nd echelon.
Letter put through the postal tracing section to ascertain to which depot and to which battalion within the depot the addressee has been posted.
If tracing section records contain information of unit to which addressee is posted letter endorsed accordingly.
[Mr. Mulock.)

Supply-Post Office
If postal tracing section records have no information letter is held and again put through the records at regular intervals.
Redirected letter forwarded to appropriate reinforcement battalion.
Battalion mail orderly sorts into companies and delivers to the addressee if he is still with the battalion.
If addressee has been posted to an advance reinforcement battalion letter is again redirected by the mail orderly.
Letter sorted by Canadian postal unit and forwarded to the advance battalion for delivery.
If addressee has been posted from advance battalion letter is put through the records to ascertain new address.
Letter redirected according to new address and transferred to Canadian postal unit for sortation and dispatch.
Letter despatched to Canadian postal unit serving the new address.
Letter dispatched by Canadian postal corps to the addressee's new unit where it is delivered by unit post orderly if the addressee is still with the unit.
If addressee has become a casualty the letter is so endorsed by competent authority.
Letter returned to the postal tracing section at Canadian 2nd echelon.
Letter put through tracing section records to ascertain where the addressee is now located.
If the records have received information letter is again redirected.
If there is no information letter is put through postal tracing section records at regular intervals until the new location is recorded, when the letter is readdressed.
After redirection letter is forwarded to the C.P.C. postal unit.
Canadian postal corps unit sorts the letter according to the new address, usually a hospital, and forwards it to the nearest Canadian or British postal unit for delivery.
It often happens that the wounded man is moved from a British to a Canadian hospital. Letter is then redirected to the new hospital by the hospital mail orderly.
Letter is forwarded through tracing section where the new address is recorded and the letter immediately sent on for delivery.
Letter is forwarded by Canadian postal unit to new hospital address.
On arrival of the letter at hospital it is delivered to the addressee if he is still in the hospital. If he has left the hospital the same procedure as outlined above is followed ad lib until the letter eventually reaches the addressee.
It will be noted that I concluded the statement just read at the point where we deal with mail for a soldier who is a casualty and in hospital.
Let me now place on record action which has been taken to improve the service to these men by short-cutting the time required for delivery.
Use of Casualty Air Mail Postcard.-To expedite mail to soldiers in hospital a special card has been introduced with the approval of the Department of National Defence.
Normally, as hon. members are aware, mail travels to the unit of address and is redirected by the mail orderly of that unit to the latest known address. This procedure is followed
until the mail is delivered to the addressee. The procedure involves many handlings and frequent searches through records before it reaches a soldier in hospital.
Now, on entry to hospital if the case so warrants-if he is going to be in hospital some considerable time-a special card is filled in either by the soldier or on his behalf asking relatives and friends when writing to him to add the words "in hospital" to the unit address which they usually use.
This card after being filled in is given priority treatment throughout the whole of its transmission to the addressee in Canada. Wherever possible, delivery is expedited by air transport without charge.
Letters mailed in Canada bearing the indication "in hospital," instead of being forwarded to the man's unit, are routed direct to the records in the United Kingdom or with the central Mediterranean Force, as the case may be.
At these points the letter is endorsed with the latest known address of the soldier and it is sent to destination by the quickest possible means.
Letters bearing the words "in hospital" are given priority treatment at the base post office and are given preference in the matter of transport according to the rate paid, air or surface.
This procedure short-cuts the normal practice of delivery to the unit and the tracing through the various steps from unit to unit and eventually to hospital.
Some of the complainants have intimated that the department has endeavoured to make financial gain out of the present situation by collecting airmail fees and sending mails by surface.
Naturally I can only speak for the mail posted in Canada to which Canadian postage is affixed. Westbound mail to Canada is the responsibility of the administration in whose jurisdiction it is mailed, but I cannot imagine any postal administration endeavouring to exploit the present situation for financial gain.
Priority is unquestionably given to mail prepaid .for air transport. It does happen, however, occasionally that meteorological forecasts indicate bad flying weather for several days ahead, or possibly mechanical difficulties will delay the take off for several days and there is no alternative aircraft available. In such cases, if there is a fast surface outlet and the possibilities are that the mails will reach destination earlier, the air mails are transferred from the plane to the surface ship. The determining factor is to secure the earliest possible delivery to the addressee.

As to the personnel angle, I have nothing but the highest of praise for the courage, devotion and determination of the crews of the Royal Canadian Air Force and the Trans-Canada Air Lines, who fly these aircraft in all weathers and who are subject to all kinds of hazards and dangers.
I have purposely gone to some length in dealing with the subject of mail to and from the Canadian armed forces as I desire to place before the committee and before the public the complete picture as clearly as circumstances permit.
As I have mentioned, I have every sympathy with the anxiety of those persons who are complaining of the delay or non-delivery of letters to and from their sons, daughters, husbands and friends. I appreciate just how they feel.
The majority of complainants, as hon. members will have gathered from the particulars of the actual elapsed times required for the

Supply-Post Office
various classes of mail, have not allowed sufficient time for their letters or parcels to be delivered and for an acknowledgment to be received.
The postal service, civil and military, has nothing to hide. We have no reason to seek excuses. There is no cause for blame. We have unfailingly striven to give the best possible service with the facilities at our disposal We have continuously striven to improve these facilities and to overcome obstacles and handicaps, always, however, with an abiding appreciation of the grim necessity of priority being given to vital supplies of men and materials necessary for the welfare and success of our arms.
In closing, I wish to pay tribute to the members of the civil postal service and the Canadian postal corps who have not spared themselves in their efforts to safeguard the mails and to expedite delivery.
The esprit de corps of the armed forces postal service is second to none. Every individual, whether in a postal unit operating near the front lines or in the base at home, is imbued with one dominant idea, that of service.
I ask every member of this house, if they have complaints which they wish investigated, to forward them, and I can assure them that such complaints will be given careful consideration, a thorough investigation, and that they will receive a report as to the results.

I wish to thank the minister for his comprehensive statement. Perhaps most hon. members will feel that it is so comprehensive and so far-reaching in its details that some time will be required to digest all the points which it raises.
It is not my purpose to deal at length with the statement, but rather to ask the minister one or two questions which have been concerning me for some time in connection with the mails. I believe that most of us who have a heavy overseas correspondence have observed considerable irregularity from time to time in the mail service. Some letters come very quickly from far-away places, but at times the delays are very great. Perhaps I shall find when I have digested the minister's statement that this point is cleared up.
One matter of complaint by our Canadian boys, of which the Minister of National Defence may have heard something when he was overseas a short time ago, is their belief that the United States mail and postal services are much more expeditious than our own. Whether that is the fact I am not in a position to say, but the statement is made repeatedly,
and I think we should have some information to show whether it is unfounded or whether there is some basis for it in fact.
Another point is this. I understand that our boys are not required to pay postage on ordinary mail coming this way, but they are charged for letters they send by air mail. I have none with me at the moment, but I received two or three such letters to-day, both from the scene of military operations and from England. Apparently the soldier has to pay airmail postage. I wish the minister would give some consideration to this matter. It seems to me that we owe it to our troops to enable them to send their letters, no matter how they are sent, without payment of any postal charges. I would not have brought this up except that I have just had one or two complaints from overseas with respect to it. It is true they were only mild complaints; nevertheless I think the matter is sufficiently important for the minsiter to deal with it.
On some subsequent occasion the minister might give us some idea of the yearly movement of tobacco from Canada to the troops overseas. I ask this question because it may be the foundation of something else which I shall want to say later on. I am not so sure that all our troops get all the tobacco that they should from Canada.
And cigarettes.

Yes. When I said
"tobacco" I used that as a comprehensive term, including cigarettes. There may be some reason to the contrary, but I do not know why the government should not provide our boys overseas with tobacco and cigarettes.
There is a small issue.

I realize that. I wish the government would take the matter under favourable consideration. As most hon. members know, some men overseas get a lot of tobacco and cigarettes. I know that a new system has been instituted whereby at a certain stage a distribution is made more equitably throughout the units. Nevertheless I think the government might give consideration to a ration issue of tobacco and cigarettes to our men. It would be a small thing from the point of view of money but a big thing so far as our troops are concerned. Both the government and civilians should be extremely generous in these matters. To some civilians they may seem little things, but to the men overseas they are greatly magnified. I should like to think that we here are doing all we can for the men in this regard, and I include cigarettes and tobacco and such other comforts as may be needed. I
Supply-Post Office

do not think it is always equitable, nor is it always just, that the men overseas should have to rely for these little additional comforts on their friends over here, because, as the minister knows, some of them have more friends here than others. I leave this suggestion with him, and when we have digested the lengthy report he has given, we shall be more competent to deal with some of the details contained therein.

May I reply to one or two questions asked by the leader of the opposition. As I understand the United States parcel system, the soldier must write and ask for articles to be sent him before they are sent. They have not been accorded the same facilities in the receiving of parcels that our troops enjoy. In regard to tobacco parcels, I might give the figures. There are 3,869,000 parcels averaging, as closely as we can tell, between 500 and 600 cigarettes to the parcel.

On the first question the minister has answered, I do not think he quite understood my reference to United States mail. I was not referring to parcels. The complaints I have had are with respect to letters, not parcels.
We will let the item stand.

I should like to say a few words on the subject of airmail service to the forces. Not only have I sent mail to the forces, but, like the hon. and gallant member for Nanaimo (Mr. Chambers), I have received a fair amount overseas. I compliment the minister upon the steady improvement in the postal service to the army, the air force and the navy overseas in the last two years. Actually, the provision of a quick mail service to the men in combatant zones is not quite so easy as some armchair critics in Canada think it is.
I have one or two little suggestions to offer the minister, first of all, about airmail letter cards, which are the most effective way of getting mail to the troops. My first objection to the Canadian form is the awkward way in which it is prepared as far as writing is concerned, because of the manner in which it is folded. One writes a little bit here, a little bit somewhere else and a little bit over on the back. The British, who started the system, have an easier way. They make one fold in the paper; it is the same sized paper, and one writes as one would an ordinary letter. The second suggestion is that the minister should revise the rates for sending these things. The leader of the opposition has suggested that perhaps all soldiers' mail should go free airmail. That is an admirable suggestion, but

I do not think it is a practical one. If you saw the amount of mail coming back you would realize that we would have to divert half the bomber group overseas to carry mail back. I think, however, that all Canadian service men overseas should have an opportunity of sending at the British overseas rate. The British man outside the country can send one of these things to Britain for threepence and the civilian in Britain sends one back for sixpence, just as we pay ten cents. A great number of Canadian soldiers in Britain must pay the sixpenny rate. In the far east and middle east we pay threepence to send one of these to Canada and from Great Britain sixpence. I suggest to the minister that he make an investigation to see whether the Canadian troops overseas could not send these airmail letter cards to Canada for threepence.

There is no rationing of these cards to civilians either in Canada or in Great Britain, but our Canadians in the middle east and the far east get a ration of only one a week. I suggest that there should be no ration. As hon. members know, the mothers and sweethearts in this country are sending bundles to Canadians to supplement the ration. I urge that there should be no ration to the men in the middle east and the far east.
May I refer to the cigarette situation. When I was first overseas there were many complaints about cigarettes, and there was undoubtedly a considerable loss both on convoy and by pilfering not only in the regular but in the army post office. I commend the minister for the way in which he cleared up that situation. Every cigarette package now coming is registered, and when it is opened by the orderly in the unit a check-up is made. Recently there

Sup-ply-Post Office
has been little loss in cigarettes delivered overseas. There is considerable delay, but, after all, parcel post going forward is not nearly as important as the letters themselves. I was interested in what the leader of the opposition said regarding the scarcity of cigarettes. It is true that some men are more fortunate than others in having more friends to send cigarettes to them, but I wish to pay a tribute to the service clubs, labour unions and various other organizations throughout the country who have contributed so heavily to provide cigarettes free for almost every Canadian overseas. If I may refer to my own experience with the Windsor City squadron, the city took such good care of us that I suggest to the minister that one of the problems which will have to be faced in connection with rehabilitation w'hen the war is over is that of teaching our chaps to buy their own cigarettes again after getting cigarettes free for so long.

I wish to give the minister notice that I propose to ask him to make a statement at a future date convenient to himself with respect to the policy of the government and of his department relating to those members of the public service belonging to the railway mail clerks' association who did not, for reasons which seemed good to them at the time, back in 1924, 1925, 1926 and 1927, take up the offer of the government of the day regarding the superannuation fund, and who are now seeking, because of a reduction of interest rates allowed on the payments they make into the retirement fund, to have a further extension of time given for their benefit, feeling otherwise that they are being discriminated against. I am giving that as a notice of motion to the Postmaster General.
May I tell the hon. member for York-Sunbury that this is a matter regarding which he should give notice to the Minister of Finance?
It is up to you. I think you ought to answer it. I am going to depend upon you for an answer.

The question that I desire to put to the minister deals with mail received by the ranks of service men in Italy. The reports I have are to the effect that men have gone as long as three weeks without any mail being received by their units. Can the minister give us, from his records, the longest period of time since December in which the men in Italy have not received mail?
Is the hon. member referring to air mail?
Mail of any kind; the men have not received mail of any kind.
In Italy?
Yes.
Could the hon. member tell me whether the people involved were in a reinforcement unit or a definite unit?
They were in a reinforcement unit.

On this occasion I suggest that the hon. member read the statement which I have put on Hansard. If he does so, he will see some of the difficulties in the reinforcement units. When this department comes back into supply on the estimates, I suggest that he bring up the matter again. I think it would be well for him to go over my statement in the meantime. I shall be glad to get the information for him. It is not available here.
It is true there have been some losses, of a definite nature, of mail going to Italy?
Yes.
I should like the minister to give the committee assurance that the mail is now being resumed and is being received at the present time.
Oh, yes.

I suppose at some later date the minister will enlarge on one or two points in particular. I took down the sequence of dates when the minister was making a statement and I gathered that ordinarily mail takes about twenty-eight to thirty days to be delivered. I followed the mail step by step as
95S
Supply-Post Office

it progresses through Canada to destination, and I find that it gets up as high as ninety days and with some slight additions it may reach a hundred days; but I would think the average would be twenty-eight to thirty days.
I was referring to parcels.

I took a note of the
statement the minister placed on Hansard, and I notice that it keeps running up until it reaches ninety days. That cannot be the regular sequence of things when the average runs to about twenty-five days or thereabouts.

I put these different figures on the statement to show what happens with regard to parcels. Parcels are treated differently from letters. I would suggest that the hon. member look over each of the differem tables. What he says about the mails is approximately correct. The parcels may not go in the same convoy or in the same ship with letters.

Parcels are just the
same. I have acknowledgments of many parcels and they ran around twenty days, and while there is a build-up here of ninety days I am trying to coordinate one statement with the actual experience.

I should like to ask the
hon. member one question. Is he speaking about parcels to the United Kingdom or to the Mediterranean?
I am speaking of parcels to the United Kingdom.

The statement with regard to ninety days applies to the Mediterranean.
Mr. LOCKHART Those run from ten to twelve days longer. May I refer to the mails coming this way, the air mail, for which a soldier has to pay. The leader of the opposition referred to that. During the past week I received four letters, two by air mail and two by regular mail. The two letters by regular mail arrived ahead of the air mail. If that is going to be the situation, I suggest either making it free to the men or cut it out altogether.

Just on that subject, I
might have mentioned that where we have space available when we are carrying air mail we bring surface mail although airmail rates have not been paid on them. ' We are going to carry all the mail we can, even if it is surface mail.

I can give the minister an example. I received a letter from Victoria,

delivered right on the battlefield, which had taken only six days. I received a cable delivered in England which had taken eleven weeks. Therefore, you can take your pick.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speechtext: The house resumed from Thursday, February 24, consideration in committee of a resolution to grant to His Majesty certain sums of money for the carrying out of measures consequent upon the existence of a state of war- Mr. Ilsley-Mr. Bradette in the chair.

5. Personnel supplies and services:	food,
medical and dental stores, clothing and personal equipment, $159,566,238.

I wish to bring a matter to the attention of the minister and ask whether he will give consideration to an improvement in the methods under which apples are being bought for the army. There used to be a ceiling imposed on prices by the Department of National Defence, which made sure that apples should not cost more than SI.65 a bushel. For purposes of this discussion we can take a box to be the equivalent of a bushel. They used to be SI.65 a bushel or a box, with the consequence that outside a certain radius from the production point it was impossible for a camp or an army establishment to purchase apples because the freight mounted up too high.
Local purchase?
In Canada, yes.
I mean, it was local purchase, it was not for Munitions and Supply under contract?

I cannot follow the minister through that because the exact method which is adopted is not clear to me. As I understand it, the restriction was put on by the Department of National Defence. As the weeks went by, storage charges, of course, mounted on those apples, and by the time they reached the point of consumption the radius was drawn back and back by the extra cost of the bushel or the box until toward the end of the season the apples were not getting outside British Columbia. I am speaking, of :ourse, of British Columbia production. They were reaching only those

War Appropriation-Army
camps which were west of the Rocky mountains. When the wartime prices and trade board put on their ceiling last year the Department of National Defence ceiling was dropped to substitute for it. The restriction then was that nothing of a higher grade than grade C was to be bought for the troops. That is the third grade of apples. If there was a restriction by grade in the purchase of other foodstuffs the producer of apples would, of course, have little grievance; but that is not the situation.
When beef is purchased for the troops Blue Label is purchased. When potatoes are purchased, the highest grade of potatoes, No. 1, is purchased. It is the same with onions; No. 1 are purchased, and with oranges nothing below fancy may be bought. In connection with apples, however, the third grade is considered good enough for the troops. The United States do not look upon this matter in that way at all; they purchase the best grade of apples for their troops. Last year when, because for export difficulties, some two hundred thousand boxes were released for export to the United States, they were commandeered by the army commissary department as soon as they arrived in that country, and moreover a commissary officer was sent to British Columbia to see to it that nothing but the .highest grades and the most desirable export varieties were sent. So that the United States take, shall I say, greater care of the requirements of their men in apples than we do.
Then in the United States and the United Kingdom there is a far more definite recognition of the nutritional value of apples than there is in Canada. In this country there was very little obtainable in the way of statistical information two or three years ago, but I am informed that some valuable work in .nutrition has been carried on by experimental farms throughout Canada, particularly the one at Summerland, British Columbia. Officials who formerly were rather skeptical of the value of apples in regard to nutrition are now in agreement that they have a value for which nothing else can be substituted. It seems to me that an attempt should be made to place the purchase of apples on a different basis. The latest arrangement, I believe, I find in a letter sent last month by the deputy minister of national defence to British Columbia Tree Fruits Limited, in which he says:
.	.	. the matter has been receiving careful
consideration and it has been decided that, until the next apple crop is harvested, this department will purchase a proportion of the higher grades of apples in both western and eastern Canada.
I cannot help thinking that this decision has been induced by the shortness of the 1943 crop, which was below average; now that we are along toward the end of February it may very well be that inconsiderable quantities of apples are available for purchase.
I am bringing this matter to the minister's attention in the very great hope that this method will not be adopted in the coming year. We are heading for an enormous crop, as we think, and it seems most desirable that our men should have the greatest possible opportunity to obtain a good and plentiful supply of apples. I do not know if the minister has received complaints from the troops, as many hon. members have, and also from the parents and relatives of men in camp in Canada. They do not see why they cannot obtain a respectable apple to eat, so that I would suggest to the minister that this matter be reconsidered. It is just too bad that only the poorer grades of apples, if they are obtainable at all, should be placed before these men. I suggest that consideration should be given to allowing greater latitude on the part of the quartermaster who purchases them. He is given a certain amount of discretion in buying his beef, his potatoes, his onions, his oranges and, for aught I know, other foods, and it seems to me that it would be quite reasonable to allow him some latitude in the purchase of apples. These C grade apples are excellent apples of their sort, but for many years the Department of Agriculture has advocated buying by grade, and if you do buy by grade you get what you pay for. These C grade apples are admirable for apple pie and applesauce, but when it comes to eating apples it is much better to pay the extra money and enable the men to have at least fancy apples, which is the next grade above C.
Of course, coming from British Columbia, I am looking at this matter from the point of view of that province, but it applies also to the other two producing centres in Canada. When there is a fixed price the radius becomes so, small that those outside that' radius do not get their apples; and if there is the further restriction that only the third grade- may be purchased, then even if the men get apples at all they do not get a palatable fruit. Would the minister give consideration to this?

Knowing where I come from, my hon. friend can, I think, be sure that I shall do so. The hon. gentleman has caught me quite off base; I do not know anything at all about this. I notice that he has correspondence with the deputy minister, but it has not been brought to my attention.
War Appropriation-Army
This was not a letter to me but to British Columbia Tree Fruits Limited, which was handed to me.

I shall look into the matter at once. I am quite satisfied that the quartermaster-general does have the discretion, but he may not have considered it necessary to exercise it. My only thought is that the C grade British Columbia apple may be as good as the first grade United States apple; that is the only suggestion I have to offer, though I hardly suppose a Nova Scotian would admit that. I have just received a note from one hon. member who tells me that the matter was taken up with my department and that just lately he was advised that the best grade is now issued to the troops. I have not personal knowledge of it, but I shall look into the matter and let the committee know. Being an inveterate apple eater myself, I thoroughly agree that the best is none too good, and agree with my hon. friend as to not oply the nutritious bht also the delicious qualities of an apple.

Could the minister give the committee some information in connection with the matter of reporting casualties? I have no knowledge of the difficulties with which the army is faced in reporting casualties to the director of records, but in a number of instances with which I am familiar the bare report has come from overseas that So-and-so has been wounded in action. The ^message that is sent out by the director of records is to the effect that this man has been reported wounded, but the extent of the injuries is not known at the time, and it is a matter of perhaps ten days or possibly three or four weeks in some instances before any further information is obtained. Could the minister not do something to obtain more details when these first casualty reports come in from the front? In one case I have in mind the man did not even have to retire from his position; he suffered merely a superficial wound, but his next-of-kin were greatly concerned when they received a message from the director of records stating that this man was wounded. As far as they knew he might have been seriously wounded. Could the minister enlighten us on that point?

Naturally this matter has given me a great deal of concern, not only in connection with the time at which the wound is reported but also in connection with the report of the nature of the wound itself. I think I have gone into it all the way up and all the way down the line. It is regarded as

most essential that information be sent to the next-of-kin at the earliest possible moment as to the fact of the casualty having occurred. A suggestion was made to me the other day by a father, who said, "I have a suggestion which sounds very simple, and I wonder that you have not accepted it long ago. That is, do not send your information with regard to the casualty until you are able to tell us the nature of the wound." I said, "My dear friends I know what would happen; within ten days somebody would wire or radio home with regard to that particular case and information would be given as to his wound before the Department of National Defence would have reported it."
I think that has happened in one or two cases.

I am afraid it has happened in more than one or two cases. There was a case of four officers that gave me a great deal of concern last October. The nature of the wound is reported just as soon as the man is brought to a centre from which a report can be sent. As my hon. friend knows, these men are out in battle. They are wounded and a stretcher-bearer comes to attend them. The stretcher-bearer takes the name and makes a note of the wound, and that is sent back as soon as possible by runner or otherwise. Battalion headquarters are notified that Smith is wounded. However, I think the medical men will agree that it would be a dangerous procedure to adopt to have the stretcher-bearer attempt a diagnosis. It could happen that he would give the impression there was only a slight wound when the soldier might be suffering from something that would result seriously.
Immediately the man gets back to the dressing-station or the regimental aid post-I forget the names, but it used to be the regimental aid post in the last war-the diagnosis ;s made by a medical man. It may happen that the man is tagged "DNK", which means "diagnosis not known". Every effort is made then to see that the man is sent back to a hospital or a casualty clearing station where a more definite examination can be made.
That is the reason for the difference in time between reporting the actual casualty and the nature of the wound. I am gratified to be able to say that these reports as to the nature of the wound have been coming through more promptly. The practice has been and still is where a wound is superficial not to load the communication circuits with information of that kind. My hon. friends will understand that the load on the transmission circuits and

.	War Appropriation-Army
the wireless with regard to operations and things of that sort is almost impossible to handle, and to load them with casualty messages would be perhaps more than the circuits could stand. As a matter of fact, we put in a special circuit from Italy to Canadian military headquarters in England to carry these particular messages.
If my hon. friends have any cases in mind- and I am not sure that they have-they would help the service if they would refer them to me. Coming back to what my hon. friend has asked about, I do not think there is anything that can be done to make the notification of the nature of the wound concurrent with the notification of the casualty. Our effort is to report promptly any casualty, and we report the nature of the wound just as soon thereafter as we can get a diagnosis that can be reasonably relied upon.
If the wound is obviously a superficial wound, would that fact be advised in the first communication sent?

They use the words
"slightly wounded" sometimes, but that is as far as they go. I suppose the stretcher-bearer might be justified in making that statement. That is the only indication I have seen of anything attempted which was not a medical description of a wound.
When air force men in Great Britain need more clothes they are provided by the British government. Does the same apply to the army?
Does my hon. friend mean when clothes are lost?
When clothes wear out the British government look after the replacements.
The policy is the same. If my hon. friend knows of a case where it has not been done, it is in error and it should be rectified.

Some of the men in the air force are complaining that the uniforms they get are much coarser than those they got from the Canadian government and I was wondering if the- same applied to the army. Will the minister tell the committee what the limit is in connection with dental supplies. I am referring to porcelain inlays for teeth. Are the men as well as the officers allowed porcelain inlays, or is there a limit according to rank:?

If there is a limit, the limit is the same for officers as for men. The 100-61
director general of dental services is not here and the director-general of medical services is giving me this information, but he is quite satisfied it is correct.
What is the limit on that?
It is the same whether you are a soldier or an officer; you get your teeth fixed in the same way.
I am asking with regard to porcelain inlays.
I cannot tell my hon. friend whether porcelain inlays are denied to officers. If they are, they are denied to the men. If they are denied to the men, they are denied to the officers.

Can the minister give, us any information as to whether the situation in regard to sending parcels to prisoners of war has improved within the last year and whether there has been any increase in the number of vouchers or special tags that are available periodically?

I just -have the information which comes from the Dieppe prisoners who were repatriated. They expressed appreciation of the service given by the Red Cross in connection with sending parcels. From the information I received the general impression seems to be that there has been a distinct improvement. Considering all the difficulties I think the service has been extremely good. I spoke with one officer who had been a prisoner of war and had been repatriated. I cannot give my hon. friend the number of tags or whether it has been increased. As my hon. friend knows, the number will be increased as the prisoners of war increase in number.

I understand that the situation as far as Red Cross parcels are concerned has improved materially, but I was thinking of next-of-kin parcels and whether, now that shipping has improved, an increase will be permitted. I sincerely hope that this will be, done as soon as possible.
The hon. member means to increase the number of parcels which may be sent? It is a question of transport.
Does the word "medical" in this vote refer to the medical inspection of recruits going into the army?

It does.
Mr. MacNICOL I have had many cases of men who have been in the army for one or two years and then been discharged. I myself

War Appropriation-Army

have written about a number of them- to the department. The wonder to me is how they ever got past the medical inspection in the first place. Some had flat feet; one had a broken foot, and there were many other cases which made it seem as if the army were taken in the halt, the lame and the blind. They would be kept in the army for a considerable length of time, at great expense to the country, and then be discharged. I should like to find out how they could ever have been passed in the first place if there were any medical examination whatever.

After my hon. friend cites a case like that, it is difficult for me to tell him what I was intending to tell him. There are very many men who are passed, and properly passed, at the time of enlistment by the medical boards, but who simply cannot take the change from a sedentary life to the activities of army life. I say this, too, in the presence of members of the air force. There are some features of army life which, as far as physical strain is concerned, are very much tougher on the man than the air force, outside of the aircrew, and some men gradually break down under the constant wear and tear of army life and of the training. That is one reason why there are many more discharges from the army than from the other services.
A second reason-and I say this advisedly- is that the requirement of physical fitness on enlistment in the army has not been so high as in the other services, particularly the air force.
The third reason-and the cases my hon. friend has in mind I think would come in here-is, as I explained to the house two years ago, that in the earlier days we had a great many civilian medical practitioners on the boards. They were doing the best they could with regard to examinations, but they were not in the army and had not had the benefit of army training, and the knowledge of army requirements. We found that a great many men who had been passed1 by these boards simply did not stand up, and that there were some cases such as my hon. friend speaks of who, if they had been examined by any army board such as we have to-day, would not have been passed1 in the first place.

Mr. Chairman, like the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), with whom I am not always in agreement, I feel that the item we are now discussing should be divided at least in two sections. One might include whatever relates to the medical corps and the drugs needed by the army, food being also covered by that first section, and the other might include clothing and personal articles.
[Mr. MacNicol.J
Referring first to food, I must say to the honourable the minister of national defence (Mr. Ralston) that it happens but too often that soldiers are poorly fed in some camps. As regards the Quebec district especially, I must tell him that complaints are often whispered-because those who make them do not want to run foul of their officers, and some soldiers are timorous-concerning the more or less cleanly and sometimes terrible conditions obtaining in some kitchens where the odours develop anything but appetite, where the colour of the tables is too often on a par with that of the floor and wh^re the sunshine wages a merciless but often vain struggle against the altogether too numerous microbes they harbour. As I have had an opportunity, while a member of the medical corps, to examine the rations, I have always been surprised to notice how first class food would, through the process of cooking, be transformed into some kind of stew not unlike the black broth of the Spartans. The best foods, if carelessly prepared, can give a very poor reputation to the cooks and their helpers without forgetting the contractors who are all no doubt anxious to supply at the lowest cost the best possible products. I have mostly heard complaints about the food at Valcartier camp, where some of the men claim that they have to rely on the canteen to fill up a stomach which, otherwise, might incur the rebellion of an ill-fed body. There is undoubtedly a lack of watchfulness somewhere, an unpardonable carelessness, or an inefficiency to which military authorities should put a stop. Soldiers are not all given to complaining; while in the army I have met very few men who did that and the reason why I consider nearly all of them reasonable is that I was making it a point to listen to what they had to say and to pay attention to their complaints.
Still, it would be interesting to hear from the minister whether among the contractors who supplied food to the Valcartier camp there was a concern by the name of Wesiberg which derived its fame from its sausage. It would also be quite interesting to know whether the wartime prices and trade board, which had something to do with that famous investigation which fizzled out, intends to punish the guilty and to cooperate with the health department, the mayor and the aldermen of the city of Quebec. While I have heard complaints about the food at Valcartier camp, on the other hand the news from the Montmagny camp are by far the best. The soldiers who have spent a fairly long time at those two camps have had an opportuntiy to notice the very great difference between them, despite the fact that both

War Appropriation-Army
are in the same district. Obviously the trouble lies in the preparation of the food, and therefore in the efficiency of the cooks. The officers of the Department of National Defence should exercise strict supervision over the manner in which kitchens are kept and over the competence displayed in preparing food. Good food brings good discipline, goes the proverb held in high honour by schoolboys. The same maxim applies equally well to the army. I recall the tour made by the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) at the beginning of the war in several camps of the Quebec district and the feeling of satisfaction evinced by servicemen when they heard that delicious pork and beans cooked in molasses would stand high on the food list. Since that time, things have inevitably relaxed, and I would ask the minister to make sure, by stern means if necessary, that our soldiers are always given the food they need.
I now come to the medical and health aspects. I do not intend to quote statistics on venereal disease or to delay the sailing of a corvette, even if it should sail from Quebec. According to an official report, Montreal and Quebec are more badly hit by the venereal evil than any other city in the dominion. This same report ascribes as principle cause of the trouble the commercialization of prostitution. I believe the report is incomplete; it should have mentioned the fact that people from all over the dominion have thronged to these two cities since the outbreak of the war. Units on their way overseas, whether they come from the neighbouring province or from the western provinces do not simply pass through; they often put in quite a stay; the findings of a report cannot be established without mention of this fact. In a gathering of men hailing from the four comers of the country and often from overseas, for Canada is very hospitable, we inevitably find different temperaments, different mentalities, ways of life which do not tally with one another, all of which clash to result in an unfortunate relaxation of behaviour favoured by the traditional bottle of beer.
On this point, opinions differ as to the best means that can be used to reduce the dangers of contamination, as far as service men are concerned. Is the lack of supervision on the part of municipal authorities in cities visited by our soldiers responsible for all the misfortunes and disasters which the medical corps, whatever its reputation, never fails to discover in military hospitals where preventive and curative means outdo each other in efficiency? Or are we to infer that the numerous means of prevention and protection with which our soldiers are provided by the army medical 100-614
authorities have caused a feeling of overconfidence bringing about hasty verdicts in the case of the most dangerous diseases developed by contact? I do not wish to venture on ground which lies outside the political sphere, as I do not care to state an opinion which is based on insufficient information. Over and1 over again, however, experience has taught me that, in the treatment of venereal disease, the army needs specialists; they should be found among medical officers, and if there are not enough of them in the army, the authorities should retain them as civilian physiciains. If the propagation of venereal disease has reached such an alarming point, I am not ready to declare that lack of moral sense among our soldiers is the main cause of that condition, There has frequently been a lack of the necessary qualifications. Indeed, all the medical men in the armed forces cannot be expected to be specialists in this particular type of treatments. The blame must not be laid upon the shoulders of the more or less competent medical officer, but upon the senior ofliicers who have placed them in a service for which they were not fully qualified.
In so far as the medical officers of training centres or companies are concerned, they are frequently over-worked either by the hospital service or by what is commonly called in the army the sick parade. It is unavoidable that out of thousands of men some may have an absolute need for medicine; they are only human, and any practitioner knows that it is not necessary to be a soldier to have such a mentality. I firmly believe, however, that they are not more numerous in the army than in civil life, and too frequently soldiers are sent back to training after being prescribed pill no. 8, 9 or 10. Too frequently, men are labelled hypochondriacs, loafers, or in common parlance, malingerers. Too frequently, the medical personnel being inadequate, those who have to bear the burden cannot take the time necessary to examine thoroughly each and everyone of these cases. As a result, the old routine practice which professional men must always guard against, takes hold1 of these officers and they are inclined to label in advance such or such soldier according to the frequency of his appearances at the sick parade. If, in order to build up a strong army, healthy men are required, it is necessary to start by supplying the army with a personnel which is adequate, well-supervised and as well-qualified as possible. I understand that, at the beginning of the war, physicians were twitted with not enlisting in sufficient numbers. But since the government compels students to volunteer, I believe that this argument no longer applies.
War Appropriation-Army

There are two or three points brought up by the hon. member to which I wish to reply. The first point was the matter of messing and cooking. He spoke generally about messing and cooking in the camps and indicated that while the food was good the preparation was not all that it should be, and he spoke of Valcartier, which he said was not as good as Montmagny. I do not know the date to which my hon. friend is referring, but perhaps he means at the time he was in the service.
I am speaking of what one hears from soldiers one meets on the street.

I visited Valcartier last
summer or fall and saw the kitchens, and I really thought a good job was being done. My hon. friend knows we are taking a particular interest in the preparation of food as well as in the quality. As he knows, we have cooking schools at Borden, and every district has an opportunity to send and does send cooks there. I do not know of any place where there could be better cooks than in Quebec where we get the benefit of the services of many cooks who have been in the lumber camps. We also have a system of messing officers in the units and not simply at headquarters, and I am disappointed to hear my hon. friend's view about Valcartier. I shall certainly look into the matter. I had an idea that under the commandant, Colonel Gaudreau, the administration was pretty good. Since cooking is a very important part of administration I shall look into the matter. I thank the hon. member for having brought it to my attention because that is the only way of knowing about it.

The complaint was not from officers but from privates.
War Appropriation-Army

I am talking about the men's mess. I did not have the privilege pf a meal in the officer's mess there.
My hon. friend referred to venereal disease and correctly pointed out that there is a considerable additional load on Quebec and particularly Montreal, because of the tremendous transient population going through there. He realizes, as we all do, that it is a civilian problem and has to be dealt with, no matter Jvhere the population may come from. All I say to him is that it does put on these communities an additional responsibility. The services are endeavouring to do all they can to help in the way of tracing down sources of infection and giving information to the civilian authorities, and real progress is being made. I am speaking of Montreal particularly; I have not as much information about the city of Quebec. The manner in which the Montreal authorities took over the matter when it was brought to their attention by Major-General Renaud gives me hope that there will be substantial improvement there.
My hon. friend spoke of precautions taken and treatment given in the army as creating a feeling of confidence. It is not intended to do that. At the same time the services cannot neglect these precautions, and the result my hon. friend speaks of is perhaps a psychological result. Certainly we shall see to it that warnings are given. These are only precautions; that is all they are, and certain risks are run.
The hon. member spoke also of military medical officers not having experience in the treatment of venereal disease. It is true that up to six months ago upon the subject of venereal diseases the army itself did not give military medical officers any special instructions. They had only such knowledge as the medical profession and schools give in the treatment of that disease; but since Colonel Williams has been in charge of the matter we have had a venereal control officer in every district and his job is to instruct the medical officers with regard to treatment. My hon. friend knows far more about the treatment of those diseases than I possibly can, but I am instructed that under the regime that has been inaugurated the treatment is very much more simple than before. The suggestion my hon. friend made, that officers did not have a long enough time to treat a patient, seems to me hardly to hold, at least in connection with V.D.G., because as I understand it that treatment is not given in hospital. A man is not taken off parade but is treated by the use of sulpha drugs and tablets and things of that sort, and there does not have to be constant attention by a medical officer.
It is all right to take pills, but direct control under a medical officer is important. -

I am pointing out that the need for constant treatment and attention does not exist to the same degree as if a man were in hospital or in a sick bay. May I say this, and I think it is something concerning which we can take satisfaction, if one can take any satisfaction in this very serious matter. We find this record, that whereas in 1940-I am speaking now of the army-the number of infections in Canada was sixty-two out of every one thousand; in 1943 that number was brought down to thirty-two out of every thousand. Therefore, distinct progress has been made. With regard to the treatment of syphilis the treatment that is given depends, as I understand it, altogether on the particular case. One cannot lay down any rule about it. As I understand it, the treatment is intermittent and there does not necessarily have to be the constant attention of the medical officer. Many of these cases are treated in hospital where, of course, the man has constant attention.
My hon. friend spoke of malingerers. I agree with him in regard to the difficulty of telling a malingerer from a genuinely sick man. There again we have tried to do something to meet the situation. As I said the other night the term "psychiatrist" was a fearsome one. I really did not understand fully what it meant, and I was a little doubtful of introducing anybody in the profession of that name into the army. These men have come into the army. We have sixty-three of them in the army at the present time. My hon. friend is a medical doctor, and he will know better than I do whether or not they are useful. I wish to say this exactly as' I understand it. In a case where the psychiatrist is called in, the medical officer examines the man who complains of a disability of some kind. The medical officer can find no reason for that disability; that is to say, by all the tests he makes he can find no reason for disability. He then has an opportunity to call in a psychiatrist. I would think the practice would be for the medical officer to consult the psychiatrist to find out whether or not in his opinion the man was a malingerer or whether it was a genuine case of disability.
My hon. friend speaks of the fact that there is danger in our assuming that men are simulating disease, are malingering, when they are really sick. He picked out the defaulter and said that the defaulter may have something wrong with him and therefore may not get a

War Appropriation-Army
square deal. We try to eliminate that in every way possible, by examining him mentally and psychologically, as well as physically.
Even if he is a defaulter he is entitled to the same kind of treatment as the other.
I thoroughly agree with my hon. friend.
That is why I submit to the minister, it is a dangerous thing in the medical profession.

I thoroughly agree with my hon. friend. I said my hon. friend picked out the worst case, not the best case. But I agree with my hon. friend that the defaulter is entitled to as good a medical examination as anybody else.
My hon. friend spoke of promotions overseas and of the fact that they are not made as rapidly as he would like.

Promotions in Canada,
not overseas.

I thought my hon. friend said that promotions were not made very fast overseas, whereas at the same time promotions were being made of men in Canada who were veterans of two wars and have never been overseas. I should like my hon. friend to bring that to my attention. I do not mind his naming individuals, if he would like to name them. I know of no case of that kind, where a man is medically fit and is a veteran of two wars and has not been overseas, unless he is a specialist or something of that kind and it has been necessary to keep him here. I should like to know of such cases.

What I wish to know is why a man who is a veteran of two wars and who has been overseas twice cannot get the promotion he deserves when he is absolutely medically fit, absolutely bilingual and has the experience.

I got my hon. friend completely wrong. My hon. friend has put up a very good case now. My only answer to him can be that the officers under whom the man works either have not considered that he was qualified for promotion or have considered that there was someone who could better fill the job even though he had not had the same experience. The fact that a man is a veteran of two wars does not necessarily qualify him for promotion if the job can be better filled by somebody else.
If my hon. friend has a case in mind I should appreciate it very much if he would bring it to my attention, because I should
like to look into it personally. I have dealt generally with most of the points my hon. friend has raised.
Has the Canadian army set up a typhus commission in Italy similar to the one set up by the United States government, in order to combat typhus in the country they are occupying?

Before the minister answers, may I say a word? I am delighted that the hon. member for Portneuf has awakened. It is quite a miracle, because he has been sound asleep for two years with regard to the medical officer business in Quebec.
I thank the hon. member for Temiscouata.
I need no thanks.
He is very intelligent, polite and delicate.
It is the law of nature.
Oh, yes, but you have some nature.

I undertsand that there is no typhus commission as such. There is a special branch of preventive medicine under the director-general of medical services, and typhus comes under that branch. Of course, my hon. friend understands that there are other diseases of a similar nature to those which are dealt with by that same branch.
Does that branch treat the civilians as well as the men in the army?
In an area like Italy?
Yes. The United States commission went into Naples and they treated 1,300,000 people.
The answer is in the negative.

What is going to happen in the territory that the Canadian army occupies if the civilians are not looked after? I say that because I have had half a dozen letters from Italy from different men, two of them officers, and they claim that life in some sections is almost unbearable owing to the fact that the lice which carry the typhus fever are there.

I am afraid I cannot give my hon. friend any further information at this stage. I have in mind-and remember that I am only surmising this from what I saw there-that the civil government control,
War Appropriation-Army

which is established, might be administering that particular operation of the medical services, and that service may come under that department. In that connection we have certain of our officers there, but they are in the civilian government administration, the allied military government of occupied territory. There are certain Canadian officers who come under that body, and I would think that probably that commission handled preventive services and that as far as civilians were concerned they would come under that administration. I am going to find out something about it.
Does the army set up in Italy fumigation services similar to that which they have in some of the training camps in order to take care of the men's clothes?
The answer is yes.
Disinfectants?
Yes.
Has the minister any information available as to cures of venereal disease by fever-therapy? Has he any idea of the percentage that can be treated and the results?

We can get statistics on that. I know of cases. I have in mind a man in regard to that matter. That treatment is given sometimes under certain circumstances. If my hon. friend wants statistics I think I can get them.

I should like to know whether it can be made a universal treatment? I do not believe it can. What percentage of venereal diseases has been treated in the army by the fever-therapy method, and what results have been obtained?
I think we can give my hon. friend that. I cannot give it now.

I think it would be of interest to the committee if we could get that information.
There is one thing more I should like to ask in connection with the induction centres at the district depots, with regard to the psychiatric examination of the incoming personnel. Could the minister say what percentage are rejected for psychiatric reasons? I refer specifically to what are termed morons, men in low mental categories. Are figures available in that connection?

There are figures which I should like to look up and check. I gave some

figures to the committee last year. The reason for my hesitation is that I do not think it would be correct to class those who happen to be rejected as morons.

I agree entirely, but I
believe there is a special classification for those below a certain mental age, and I think "moron" is the official term used.
I will get the information.

In the case of soldiers being invalided home, is any advance notice given to the relatives where the injuries are of a very serious nature, such as multiple amputations, facial deformities and, so on? I am told that some men have been met at the station by their relatives and that sometimes the meetings have had disastrous effects. Might it not be advisable in some instances to have the first meeting take place after the soldier is comfortably in hospital?

I am glad that question is
asked, because yesterday I was chasing down a rumour that I heard, and I shall tell the committee what it was. It was stated that at a certain station here, and the station was named, a man who had both arms and both legs amputated was carried off the train, and that his relatives had not been advised of it.

I heard the same
report.

I tried to run down that rumour, and the director-general of medical services has looked into it also. We can find no such case. I will tell the committee of what may be the case which gave rise to this rumour. That was the case of a man who lost both his arms while on manoeuvres in England; he pulled the pin of a hand grenade and it blew off both arms. I saw that man in England myself. When I came home I wrote his wife about him, and I know she was aware of the extent of his injuries. I took a personal interest in that case, with particular reference to the possibility of getting appliances for that man before he came home. If my hon. friend can give me any information that will enable me to track down that report I should be very grateful, because I do not believe such a case exists.
Of course the point is that if there should be such a case, could not precautions be taken to lessen the effect upon the relatives?

Certainly they could. The committee will understand that the relatives would be advised in the regular course of hospital reports just what the accident or disability was. I felt very badly about this man

War Appropriation-Army
coming home without appliances. The provision at that time was that appliances were not issued on the other side because they wanted them fitted here; but I cabled over aqd and made special arrangements so that he had the appliances and used them on the boat before he arrived here. As a matter of fact, I had exactly the same case in my own battalion in the last war. Hon. members of the committee may know that to-day this young man is secretary of the Saskatchewan law association, having put himself through college even with that disability. I felt sure I could give some comfort to the wife of this man if I called that fact to her attention.

I wish to ask the
minister a question in regard to the matter of services. There is in Toronto a voluntary organization that meets casualty trains as they come in, bringing the relatives of the men on board. Sometimes it is three or four o'clock in the morning when the train comes in, but they bring the wives and1 children of the men to meet them. Of course there is only one way to take care of them, namely, to drive them to the station and then drive them home.
That is the wives and children?

Yes. Some time ago I had some correspondence with the minister about the matter. I know the service the members of this organization are performing, and I want to pay a tribute to them for it. I was wondering if satisfactory arrangements had been made in connection with getting gasoline to carry on this work, because, after all, many of these people only have "A" ration books, and when they have to go twenty or thirty miles out into the country to get these people and take them home it means quite a lot. Has any arrangement been made so that the members of this organization may be able to carry on their work?

I cannot tell my hon. friend whether any arrangement has been made, but I shall see whether that is possible. I agree with him that a very worth-while work is being done by the Red Cross, the women's voluntary organizations and other organizations, depending, of course, upon which organization is functioning in a particular locality. I have particular knowledge of the work being done in Halifax when these men are brought off the boats. Just the other night I had a report from the district officer commanding in connection with the arrival of the last hospital ship, and certainly everything that could be done to give care and comfort to those men was done by these loyal 100-62
people who saw these casualties of ours on board the hospital trains. However, I shall look into the matter of gasoline.
What is included in the expression, "personal equipment"?
That is the actual personal equipment of a man. It is the steel helmet, the web equipment, the ground sheets and the anti-gas equipment.
It has nothing to do with rifles, for instance?
No.

I should like to inquire a little further about this psychiatry business; it rather intrigues me. The minister stated that there were sixty-three psychiatrists in the service. How many of them are in Canada, and how many are overseas? When is the psychiatrist called in, and is that done on the advice of the medical authorities? As I understand it, a psychiatrist is not one who prescribes medicine.
Oh, yes, he does. They are qualified medical practitioners.

No doubt that is so, but they specialize in mental disease; that is their particular line in the service. What I am trying to get at is when it is considered necessary to call in a psychiatrist, and whether it is done solely on the recommendation of the medical officer who is charged with the exclusive responsibility of looking after the medical end of it. I am trying to find out just what purpose this particular officer serves. I have in mind one of the first psychiatrists to practise in Canada, Doctor Cathcart. He was brought here from England in 1920 and attached to the Canadian pension commission; and our experiences with that gentleman were not altogether happy. When the pension committee sat in 1940 this subject was thoroughly discussed, as to the application of that particular branch of medicine in connection with the determination of pensions. I think it was almost unanimously agreed by that committee that this line of service was being dispensed with because the particular clause in the act had been removed under which the psychiatrists had operated in the past. Some qualified medical men appeared before the committee and expressed the opinion that in the past it had not been a very satisfactory service. There are sixty-three of these men in the Canadian service-I assume there are not any on the other side because, if a man is mentally and physically equipped to cross the water, he should be all right. What I am trying to

War Appropriation-Army

determine is what makes it necessary for the medical authority in a unit or a camp to send a man to a psychiatrist. What conditions must prevail? When the psychiatrist makes a decision, to whom does he report? Who is the judge as to whether the particular examine tion is the last word? I know back in 1920 and 1921 many of the pensions which had been given for nervous disabilities were discontinued in a sweeping manner, but they were restored later on by the medical authorities in the different military districts. I am simply trying to determine the mechanics in connection with this. I know I am not qualified to pass judgment, but I should like to know something about it.

That is something of a technical nature, and it has developed, I do not know just how recently. I know Doctor Cathcart to whom my hon. friend has referred. This has developed just as personnel selection has developed, and it is an important development. It is something like the personnel manager in business who did not exist twenty years ago but who exists to-day. These men are referred to the psychiatrists as specialists, just as men are referred to chest or eye specialists. When a medical officer fears that a man may have difficulty in making a mental adjustment to life in the army he is referred to a psychiatrist.
He determines his mental condition.
Not his mental condition, his emotional outlook.
His state of mind.

His state of mind and the possibility of his adjusting himself. I have not been examined myself, but the director-general of medical services is on the floor and I am sure he is listening to this discussion. He belongs to this profession as well as being a medical officer. I believe I have described correctly the use which is made of the psychiatrist, particularly in the army. I am advised by prominent medical men who are not psychiatrists that these men have performed a very useful function and that they have saved us from having a good many men discharged because of mental conditions, particularly nervous conditions. I believe Doctor Cathcart's full title is neuropsychiatrist, or something of that kind, which would indicate that he deals with nervous as well as mental conditions.

Would the minister
describe hypertension?
Item agreed to.

Hypertension is high blood pressure, and hypotension is low blood pressure.
6. Signal and wireless equipment, line construction, etc., $23,599,633.
Is radar being used by the army at all, and has it been found satisfactory?
It is used extensively.

I
understood that it had not been found as useful in the army as on the sea.

I am using the word in the generic sense of referring to the various radio equipment used for purposes of detection. It is used extensively in connection with anti-aircraft. As my hon. friend probably knows, a great number of equipment installations have been turned out in Canada at a place not far from where he lives.
Does this item cover equipment for use in Canada for training purposes, or Hoes it just cover equipment being used in Europe?

Both in Canada and Europe and in Italy. It covers all signalling and wireless stones, including searchlights, cable layers, fullerphones, telephone sets, switchboards, charging sets, generators, reception sets, wireless sets, wireless stations, wave-meters, radio direction finding equipment, and so on.
Have many pieces of intercommunication equipment been purchased? I refer to the equipment by which an officer can talk back and forth with the field.
That is known as C-58. I cannot tell my friend how many.
They do not need wires?
"Walkie-talkie" is the slang term.
Can the minister say whether or not his department assisted in the construction of the telephone line for Cheti-camp to Pleasant Bay in Inverness?
Yes.

Does the minister have the figures?

War Appropriation-Army

I thought it was 85,000, but the officer here tells me he thinks it was $3,000. This was to assist in the construction of a telephone line as part of the aircraft defence corps operations in that particular part of the province.

Item agreed to.
7.	Ammunition and bombs, $182,194,664.
Could the minister give a break-down of this item?

This includes small arms and other ammunition. The round figures are as follows:
Small arms	 $48,000,000
Gun ammunition	 86,000,000
Miscellaneous ammunition		46,000,000
The last item includes dummy bombs, grenades, demolition bombs, guncotton, ammunition instruments and gauges.
How does the minister explain the large reduction this year?
Because of the tremendous stocks we have on hand which have not been used.
Overseas and here?

Overseas and here in
Canada. Perhaps I had better not use the word "tremendous." We have large stocks.

I was just going to ask a question along the lines of that asked by the hon. member for Yale. When I was home I met a number of folk who had been employed in an ammunition plant. If the minister thinks he should not answer the question I am going to ask, it will be all right. They told me they had been laid off. I asked why, and the reply was that apparently there is sufficient ammunition on hand to fight a war for ten years more. I have been wondering if that reply given to me is right, and whether this reduction of $91,000,000 is an indication of what is happening in so many plants that heretofore have been engaged in making ammunition of one kind or another. I find that the same thing is taking place in other plants making machine-guns and equipment of that kind, in which there seems to be a general reduction in production, and the reduction in the vote would seem to indicate that. Will there be a continuous reduction in production?

Production in 1943M4 was so heavy as to cover, I think, practically all the initial requirements; that is, there is a very- large stock per gun as an initial provision, and in addition there is provision for 100-62i
reserve and wastage. In 1943-44 we have, to some extent, produced reserves of some types of ammunition, and the production now is for reserve and wastage.

Item agreed to.
8.	Armament, including rifles, machine guns, mortars and guns of all descriptions, $104,819,202.

I have a question to ask on that, but I do not want the minister to answer if he thinks he should not. In Toronto a plant has been manufacturing a very large number of machine guns and other equipment of that nature. It has been rumoured-I am not able to say if it is so-that there has been a large reduction in employment at this plant, which again would indicate that a surplus has been built up and that there may be a continuous reduction in production in the goods covered by this item. Is that correct?
There has been a reduction in some items but not in others.
That would indicate that the information given me was correct.

The largest reduction is in the larger guns, 25-pounders, howitzers, and so on. There is a considerable increase

I am not giving the committee the amount-in the production of machine-guns. A very large order was placed for a certain type of machine gun. I am not so sure, having regard to recent word that I have received, that that order will be filled, but provision is made for it in case the equipment is needed. As a matter of fact, I think a substitution is being made for guns already on hand. In small arms there is a very slight reduction in rifles, for instance.
Can the minister, without any breach of security, give us a rough break-down of small arms production?
Small arms include pistols, rifles, smoke generators, anti-tank rifles, signal pistols and Piats. Does my hon. friend agree with that pronunciation?
I thought the Piats were included in the mortar category.
Has there been a steady reduction in the manufacture of machine-guns?

The provision here is for a considerable increase in the manufacture of one type of machine-gun, a large type. I was saying a moment ago that there is another of that same type of gun on hand, but word which has been received recently makes me think that possibly the amount provided here
War Appropriation-Army

for the manufacture of a certain number of these guns will be very considerably reduced because of lessened production.
What I was wanting to get was an approximate break-down of guns and mortars, two-inch mortars, and so on.

The small arms are pistols, rifles, smoke generators, anti-tank rifles, signal pistols, Piats. The machine-guns include, light, medium and heavy guns and machine carbines. The light machine-gun is in the general classification of machine-gun, not in the small arms, as I may have said inadvertently. Guns, howitzers and mortars include all types of guns, howitzers and mortars, with or without mountings, and bomb-throwers, predictors-the latter being used in anti-aircraft work.

Item agreed to.
9.	M.T. vehicles:	trucks, tractors, trailers,
tanks, A.F.Vs., and repair parts, $274,068,547.
Does this item include the vehicular equipment that is piled up and has been piled up in boxes for quite a long time on practically all the sidings all across this province?

This does not cover those vehicles. Those vehicles are on British order and constitute a reserve which is awaiting shipment. The British keep a very large backlog. I could give my hon. friend the number of motor vehicles at present awaiting shipment on sidings. What I said about a heavy British backlog applies also to their spare parts. We have literally acres of space which are filled with boxes of spare parts which could be used over a period of two years. They are awaiting shipment and will be shipped in due course.

Apparently they are
motorcars of one kind or another.
That is right; trucks, and so forth.
All that is British equipment?
