What is stored and awaiting shipment is practically all British. I am advised that the proportion of Canadian equipment is extremely small as compared with the British. I understand that they are awaiting special ships to take that particular kind of cargo across.
Where is the backlog of Canadian vehicular equipment stored?

We have reserves in
England, and, as I say, a small proportion of

what my hon. friend sees in the different locations is part of the Canadian backlog. As my hon. friend knows, a very large proportion- I would not say a majority but a substantial proportion-of British units are equipped with Canadian vehicles.
Do the words "repair parts-" appearing in the item, refer to repair parts in repair plants like the large plant at East London and plants in other parts of the province?
Is the question whether those spare parts are for use, in those plants?
Yes.

As my hon. friend probably knows, there are two classes of spare parts. One is the box or boxes of first year's spares, accompanying the vehicle; the other is the second year's spares, which are stored separately. Those are the spares to which I referred a minute ago when I said we had literally acres of buildings filled with these spares, for the British backlog.
By this time next year, if the war continues, they will be very greatly reduced?
It depends. Do I understand that my hon. friend asks whether or not we can expect that this year the item might be substantially reduced?
No. It is reduced this year. The next year.

It is reduced this year because we did not use, as we expected to do, the initial equipment which was made up. Of course a certain amount of it has been used fn manoeuvres and in general training, but I would anticipate that the wastage which we planned for will take place and that next year we shall have to fill in as we did this year, and replace the wastage out of reserve.
The Department of National Defence send their orders to the Department of Munitions and Supply, do they not?
Yes.

As regards obsolescence of equipment, an order goes in and Munitions and Supply issue instructions for a certain quantity; it is being manufactured, but things are moving quite a bit these days, so what happens in order to prevent overproduction of obsolete stuff? What is the procedure?

War Appropriation-Army
That is, if there has been a change of design in the course of manufacture?
Either a change of design or something goes out of use. It is a question of preventing waste.

We simply have to stop that. If a change of design comes into effect suddenly, what is done is to try to make plans for a change-over to the new design as of a certain date. We did that in connection with tanks, as a matter of fact. So many tanks were to be made of an existing pattern. In the meantime provision was made for the tooling up for a new pattern; that is, for the changes in order to turn out the new pattern; and as of a certain date we started the manufacture of the new type. My hon. friend will understand that when I say "a new type" it does not mean a brand-new turret; but if the ring was larger or the stowage space was changed or the signal equipment was changed, there might also have to be a different foot-plate. In large changes, changes which would be very difficult to make in the course of running a certain number of turrets or a certain number of tanks, it is better to have certainty and run so many rather than to change over all at once.
What I have in mind is this. If an article becomes obsolete, does the department say to Munitions and Supply, "we don't want it any more"? Do you cancel it right away, or what?

I do not think the word "obsolete" is quite a fair term to use in connection with most articles of military equipment which are actually in process of being turned out. There are improvements like the rifle, Marks I, II and III; there are improvements in tanks like Marks I, II and III, but Mark III is not obsolete because of the fact that Mark IV is being turned out; Mark III can be used and is being used; and not only would it be bad economics, but the troops might be left without equipment if we said, "all Mark III is out; start manufacturing Mark IV". There has to be a gradual transition from one to the other.

I do not want to hold the committee up unnecessarily, but this is an item of considerably over a quarter of a billion dollars. Could the minister give some idea of the percentage of this that goes_ in, say, armoured fighting vehicles such as carriers, tanks, and artillery vehicles, dragons, and ordinary M.T.? If the figures are available I think the committee would be interested, provided that the information does not transgress any security regulation.
My hon. friend is asking about armoured vehicles vis-a-vis the ordinary commercial vehicles?
Track vehicles and fighting vehicles and purely M.T.
I would say that the percentage is as three to two-A.F.Vs. three and commercial vehicles, two. When I say commercial vehicles I mean load-carrying vehicles.
What the Americans call prime movers and ordinary wheeled vehicles.
I am not familiar with that term, but load-carrying vehicles vis-a-vis A.F.V. are two to three.
Would you call the dragon or the artillery carrier an A.F.V.?
It is a "B" vehicle in the load-carrying vehicle class, not in the A.F.V.

I have been in a number of plants lately in which I have seen considerable quantities of valuable and expensive material which now, apparently, is not to be used, and I have been wondering how in the world all this stuff was ordered. Presumably a requisition comes in to somebody in the department who in turn issues an order. On what basis does the man who issues the requisition issue it? From whom does he get the order to issue it? Are his requisitions checked? If so, how do these considerable quantities of material accumulate in plants? I have lately been in a number of plants, and from every plant in Canada, I assume, material is being turned over to this new crown company to sell. Private business could not very well pile up material like that-material which is not going to be used-and remain in business.

Let me say that generally changes of that kind are due to changes in war conditions which have necessitated changes in the war establishments of equipment. I will give my hon. friend one instance: I dealt with it the other night after I left the house. We had ordered 2,400 of a certain kind of gun. Requisitions were put in and material assembled, and I have no doubt that some machining was done on it. Suddenly we got a wire that a change in war establishment called for something like 366 instead of 2,400. This resulted from conditions which I could explain to my hon. friend and which would be understood readily by him and by the rest of the committee, conditions which had not been foreseen. The war has improved in that' particular sphere, and as a result a change has been made. Consequently there has been a cancellatic., which means, of course, that
War Appropriation-Army

there will be some wastage in machining and things of that kind. The instance I mention will not be the only one. There are on my desk all the time cancellations which involve changes of this kind. The war was going a certain way, and when certain activities were anticipated, orders were put; otherwise I would have been "on. the mat" for not having the equipment. The situation has changed and, as a result, the necessity for equipment, and cancellations have been made. I would like to know that plant. Is my hon. friend sure in that case that the material is not going to be used?

I do not care to give the name of the plant because all the information was given me in confidence, and I am not finding fault with it, having had a lot to do with business, so that I appreciate the fact that there will be many changes in design. It would mean, however, that much material purchased would be left lying there. The information given me is that when the new crown company is set up to sell the material-I do not know whether it has been announced in the house that it will be set up-
The War Assets Corporation?
Has it been set up in the house?
I do not think it has.

It is going to be, because there was something in the newspaper about it this morning. I presume that company will endeavour to sell this material. From what I saw of this material lying around, when this new company is set up it should at once get possession of warehouses somewhere, so that this material, which is first class, can be stored and sold at some future time.

What was set up was Crown Assets Allocation Committee, and the handling is done by War Assets Corporation, which is now being set up. That has to do not simply with equipment of properties and things of that kind, and I know that the services are busy dealing with the items referred to by the hon. member for St. Paul's, which can be regarded as completely obsolete. Those are the only items which the services feel justified in discussing with the Crown Assets Allocation Committee at the present time, because we do not know how long the war will last and we do not propose to hand over to War Assets Corporation any of that material until we know that it is obsolete.

Does the army buy the planes or gliders that carry

paratroopers, or are they controlled by the air force? They are called Hannibals.

Referring to the disposal of crown assets by War Assets Corporation, or whatever body will have the disposition of these assets when the war is over, or while it is on, I had two suggestions during the past month from men overseas at the front who are anxious that all the jeeps should not be disposed of before they come back. Apparently there is a considerable demand, which has gone through the forces to a great extent, because if I have had two requests I am sure that members from all parts of Canada must have been showered with similar suggestions. I think the minister ought to give consideration to this particular suggestion, because, after all, there is really nothing too good for those who have been fighting for us, and if they have a desire for some of the equipment we ought, in our arrangements for its disposal, to consider their wishes.
I will take a note of it.
Is the same anxiety exhibited by those who want tommyguns?

Item agreed to.
10.	Operating cost of mechanical transport: Fuel, maintenance, etc. (not including repair parts), $30,044,487.

I wish to ask a question with reference to gasoline. In visiting camps and plants of one kind or another I have observed what appears to be great wastage in the use of gasoline. For instance, if an officer or a manufacturer wants to get information in Ottawa he jumps into a plane and flies to Ottawa, and that takes a considerable quantity of gasoline. His errand might or might not be of any great importance, necessitating his coming at that speed. He might have taken a train to come here. When you take the aggregate, according to the information given me, the wastage in gasoline is terrific, through the use of aeroplanes going back and forth on journeys that may or may not be of particular consequence.
Heaven forbid that I should criticize the air force with regard to the use of planes-
I am not speaking of the air force but of military officers.

The air force have been more than considerate to the army and to the minister particularly in connection with the use of planes. I do not know of any cases and I should like to look into the matter, but I may say to my hon. friend that the

War Appropriation-Army
instructions are definite to officers not to use planes or cars if/ trains can be used, unless time can be saved which it is necessary to save. I do not know what case my hon. friend refers to, but I do not think they jump into planes every time they want to go anywhere. As I understand it, flying in planes must receive the approval of national defence headquarters except in the case of the minister, who gives his own approval. This is a new one. I expected my hon. friend to complain of the use of military cars, because I hear that all the time; but I did not know that military officers were using planes excessively.
I do not mean an officer on active service, but an officer stationed at some plant-
Speaking at some plant?
Stationed at some plant. I am not referring to the fighting service.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. Does he mean a civilian officer?
I would not know whether he was a civilian or not, but an officer associated with the government in some way in a plant that has to do with the making of planes. He might be an inspector. ,
He uses a plane to go from there to somewhere else?
He flies here or elsewhere, wherever he may wish to go.
That is not my family; that is all I can say.

Has the minister come to any set routine about accidents between military and civilian vehicles? There used to be a great deal of trouble. Has any formula been worked out? At one time the crown assumed no obligation for an accident. I do not know whether fiat had to be obtained to sue the crown. Has this matter been settled, and, if so, what is the formula?

Either by passing an order under the War Measures act, or by statute, I do not remember which, that situation was altered last year and provision was made so that action can be brought, as I remember, as if the soldier were the employee of a private corporation. That is the effect of it, but I shall have to look up the act. I am sure, however, the change has been made and we have had the greatest success in the settlement of claims. We have a procedure which is working well whereby meritorious claims are settled without action at all. In England we have a claims commission; in the United
States we settle in a similar way, and they have been successful from the point of view both of the claimant and of the department.
May I ask what part of item No. 10 is gasoline?

It is all gasoline, oil, grease, anti-freeze. That includes not only loadcarrying vehicles, but tanks and other armoured fighting vehicles as well. As my hon. friend sees, there is a decrease of about $5,000,000; that is attributable to reduction in the number of vehicles in the home war establishment, and a reduction in operating cost.
As I understand it, there is nothing in this item which has to do with overseas operations?

Eighty per cent is for
overseas.
That is the entire vote for fuel and mechanical transport cost, operating cost, maintenance, et cetera, not including repair parts.
It includes overseas and all theatres of operation.
In that amount how much is for fuel?
The minister mentioned water transport. Does he mean assault landing craft and tank landing craft?
I mean the little boats for water transport. We have one of them at least in Halifax harbour, I think.
There was a mail service in Nova Scotia as well?
There is a boat up the British Columbia coast from Vancouver, too.
Yes; it does not include the tank landing craft and the assault landing craft?
It will include that, I think, yes. As a matter of fact, about eighty per cent of this item is for overseas. I would think it would include that.
The minister said that he would get me some information.
Did my hon. friend ask another question?
I asked what part of item No. 10 was fuel?

I am sorry I cannot give my hon. friend the information at the moment. As a matter of fact, the gasoline, oil, grease and anti-freeze for overseas are all under a
War Appropriation-Army

capitation rate with the British government; that is to say, it is all paid on a per diem basis. The cost of fuel gasoline in Canada is something like $4,000,000. Part of the oil is for fuel and part is for lubricating, but I cannot break it down.
I was not anxious to have any special break-down, but I should like to have some idea as to how much fuel is being used, perhaps for other reasons, as the discussion progresses.
I cannot give my hon. friend what proportion of that big item for overseas is fuel as compared with the other. It is all lumped together.
I think the minister has given me sufficient information now.
Did I understand the minister to say that the amount of fuel, gasoline, is only $4,000,000?
In Canada, yes.
This is not for outside Canada?

I said the item was $30,000,000 altogether; of that, $24,000,0000 represents estimated overseas expenditures. I cannot break that down for the committee into oil, gasoline and anti-freeze, because that $24,000,000 is based on what we call a capitation rate, which we pay the British government for servicing our troops at so much a day. They provide the oil, lubricants, and everything else. They do not measure out the gallons. They say, "We will provide you with oil, lubricant, anti-freeze and so on at a per diem rate." I have here the amount for gasoline in Canada. It is $4,000,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
Mr. Chairman, you are getting along very nicely. We have voted almost $1,500,000,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am doing the best I can. I do not want to urge the committee in any way, shape or form. However, when I think the time is ripe to call an item I call it.
We are doing our best to help you. It struck me that the amount of $4,000,000 was a very small amount if it includes the fighting equipment in Italy and the ships at sea everywhere.
Not ships.
Not the ships; but it includes all the theatres in which our men are fighting?

It includes the fighting
material.
It does?
It is a capitation method.
I thought it would have been very much more; we have so many troops there.
The amount of $24,000,000 is all that is chargeable under this head by the British government.
That covers the whole business?
That is right.
So far as gasoline and oil is concerned with respect to Canada's war effort in the old country and in Europe?
I have the exact rate and the number of days. It is all charged on a capitation rate.

Item agreed to.
11.	Sundries, including printing, stationery, telephones, telegrams and other costs not included in above items, $24,246,593.

I have a question I should like to ask and I do not see any other item on which to ask it. What has been the actual cost of recruiting for the army? H we have the actual cost for the army we might break it down per capita. I do not know whether it is figured out on that basis or not. I had in mind recruiting officers, their offices and staffs. I think the whole business has been rather costly to this country for the results obtained. I have in mind recruiting parties that go through the country. They have an officer, an N.C.O. and in some cases two or three C.W.A.C.S. They come into a community and operate dances in it. They hire a hall and pay for an orchestra. In some instances they do not get any recruits. These are actual facts. That, coupled with the coloured posters and the printing, I am sure, costs this country quite an item. I believe there should be a different system worked out, a system which would not be nearly so costly in man or woman hours or dollars and cents per recruit obtained. I should like to have those figures.

I have not the figures of the number of men who are involved. But I wish to say to the committee and to my hon. friend that I do not agree with him for a single instant. I say that it costs this country two or three million dollars every time there is a loan to influence and to persuade the peo-

War Appropriation-Army
pie of Canada to subscribe their money to the loan. I suggest that if it costs $1,500,000 to get 48,000 or 50,000 men to volunteer who may be called upon to give their lives for this country it is worth it.
Hear, hear.

I say to my hon. friend that I do not think it lies in the mouths of any one of us to say it is too much. It seems to me that we underrate the value of recruiting and the value of volunteering. If we had half the effort put into recruiting that is put into those war loans to get people to subscribe their money for a perfectly good bond, we would have a good deal more recruiting than we have. When I see what is done in the way of war loans-and I do not deprecate it in the slightest, for it is a fine thing to have us stir up the enthusiasm of our people-I do not think too much is done for recruiting. In war loans we lend our army equipment; we do everything we possibly can. What for? In order to influence our citizens to subscribe for a perfectly good bond with the promise of the Dominion of Canada to pay it back in twelve or fifteen years. If we do a little of that sort of thing in order to persuade men to enlist in the army, to give their lives for their country, I do not think parliament should be at all niggardly in the way of voting that money.
What did the minister say the cost was?

I thought the figure just included the posters, and that sort of thing, but it includes the personnel as well, and the cost in 1942-43 was $1,290,000 in round figures. The cost for the first nine months of the current fiscal year, as it has been figured out here, including personnel, was $1,138,000. That is about half the cost of one war loan.
How many recruits were obtained?
About forty-eight thousand.
Would the minister say why this item is up $10,000,000 this year?

The increase in the cost of printing and stationery is due to higher per man cost overseas; special training equipment has been increased, and there is a large increase in sundries, due principally to an increase of $6,500,000 for telephone and wireless construction and maintenance, which was formerly included under operating expenses of property. That $6,500,000 is the big item in the increase of $10,000,000.
Are these elaborate recruiting huts which are stationed all over the country still in use? There is one near the cenotaph in Ottawa, and I wondered if they were all still in use.
I understand that the one in Ottawa to which my hon. friend refers is the recruiting hut for the C.W.A.C.
That has been changed over, has it?
It has been used for that purpose for the best part of a year, at least.
Are they being used for that purpose all over the country?
I do not know; I have not seen any others.
The minister has not a break-down of the cost of operating those huts?
No, but I think the cost would come under this item.

Item agreed to.
Sundry services, $22,315,827.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I should like to know from the minister and the committee whether the sub-item should be considered individually, or whether the items will be taken together.
Will the minister explain this item?

Certainly. There is an experimental station at Suffield, for which $1,916,810 is provided. Internment operations will cost $3,730,717; the inspection board of the United Kingdom and Canada, $10,589,000; departmental administration, $1,774,000; dependents' allowance board, $805,300 and dependents' supplementary grants fund-that is, the dependents' board of trustees-$3,500,-000. The total is practically the same as last year. It is pointed out to me that these figures are not strictly comparable, due to changes in accounting procedures resulting in different groupings of expenditures in the various years, and this really applies to all the items with which we have deen dealing.
Is the experimental station new this year?
No; that was bought two years ago. This is the operating cost.

This is the first time it has been shown in the item.
. War Appropriation-Army
It was included last year in part A-army services.

I should like to ask a few questions with regard to the Suffield experimental station. In the first place, it is presumed to be a permanent station, and the question of building a few cottages as homes for the officers has come up from time to time, but nothing has been done. Then there is a rather more serious problem, in that the block takes in quite an area where the grass is fairly good, while the grass outside that area has been eaten off. A large part of this area is not being used for experimental purposes, according to my information, and those on the borders of the block who are so short of grass find it very exasperating, when they cannot get grass, to see that the grass within this field is not being used. There is also a more serious problem agitating the minds of the people of that locality, that is, the two prairie fires which were started within the area and which spread far beyond it. I personally saw a fire over a distance of forty miles, at least twelve to fifteen miles deep, which burned a lot of valuable grass. These people feel that they should be compensated for the loss of this grass, but month after month goes by and no compensation is given. I should like the minister to offer some indication as to whether their case is in good standing and whether they can hope to get any compensation for their loss.

My hon. friend has spoken of two things. I shall look into the matter of cottages. In point of fact I have not been near Suffield for nearly nine months at least, perhaps longer, but I shall look into that question. When he speaks of compensation on account of fire I presume he means fire which started within the area?
Yes.
That matter has not been brought to my attention previously. Certainly it sounds as if it had some merit, but I do not want to say anything definite. I shall look into it personally.
It has been before the officers of the department.
There must be some "catch" in it that I do not know about, but I shall look into it personally.
What would be covered in the last item of 83,500,000 for the dependents' supplementary grant fund?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I asked the minister and the committee whether these subdivisions
of the last item should be discussed separately or all together.

I have read all the items and, as I understand it, hon. members are asking questions about them. I am perfectly satisfied with that procedure. The item of
83,500,000	is to provide for the amounts to be paid out by the dependents' board of trustees by way of supplementary grants. As I said, this is a round figure. The amount paid out last year was $1,285,000.
I just wondered if it came under the trustees.
Yes.

Under what section
could I discuss the matter of proving ranges? I have been trying to find the appropriate item, though I suppose I could have asked the question at almost any time.
I think that would come under the inspection board, which is included in this item.

Then what will be done in cases where damage is being done to property in close proximity to these ranges? Has any policy been laid down? There is a matter I want to take up seriously in that connection, and I should like a little guidance on it.

Another hon. member
asked me the same thing. Is my hon. friend talking about the proving range near Hamilton?
No, it is near St, Catharines.

If my hon. friend will take it up with me I shall be very glad to look into it. As a matter of fact, I have not dealt with any of these cases at all; they have been dealt with by the inspection board. Any case that is thought necessary to be referred to the department comes to the deputy minister, but I shall look into anything my hon. friend cares to take up with me. Damage has been done by what; by concussion?
Yes, damage to nearby property by the concussion.
I shall look into it.

I think the minister will agree that we have made pretty good progress

Northwest Staging Route
on his estimates to-night. A number of questions may arise to-morrow, as we finish with his department, but I should like to make a suggestion which may facilitate the discussion and bring it to an end more quickly. Would he mind giving a statement in a simplified form as to how many N.R.M.A. men there are in the Canadian army. I have listened to my hon. friend give details of the duties performed by these men, but I am not just clear as to the actual total.

I will make a guess now which I will confirm later. There are between
70,000	and 73,000; I think I said over 70,000 before, but I will confirm that. The committee does not want to pass this item tonight?

I think not. We have made pretty goc d progress. Do not kill the goose that lays the golden egg.
Item stands.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Tuesday, February 29, 1944
